title: Bridging the antiviral gap: A BAC-based non-infectious SARS-CoV-2 replicon reveals potent antisense gapmers.
abstract: To facilitate studies of SARS-CoV-2 replication and antiviral drug discovery, we developed a non-infectious SARS-CoV-2 replicon, pBAC-SARS-CoV-2_S/eGFP_ΔE, based on a bacterial artificial chromosome vector. The viral genome was modified to ensure non-infectivity while allowing replication monitoring: the spike (S) protein and envelope (E) protein open reading frames (ORF) were deleted, and ORF S was replaced with an enhanced GFP (eGFP) reporter. Upon transfection, the pBAC-SARS-CoV-2_S/eGFP_ΔE was replication-competent in HEK293T cells and was inhibited by remdesivir, validating the replicon utility for studying SARS-CoV-2 replication and antiviral screening. RNA structures regulate the SARS-CoV-2 replication cycle by controlling genome stability, expression, and interactions with viral and host proteins. Using the pBAC-SARS-CoV-2_S/eGFP_ΔE, we evaluated antisense gapmers targeting RNA structural motifs within the untranslated regions (UTRs) and nucleocapsid (N) and membrane (M) genes. Screening identified five potent gapmers: one targeting the 5' UTR, three targeting the N gene, and one targeting the M gene. The M-directed gapmer was the most active, with an EC50 of 6.3 nM, highlighting the M coding region as a promising antisense target. Four of the identified gapmers, including the lead, recognize accessible motifs present in both genomic and subgenomic RNAs, suggesting that dual targeting may be an effective antiviral strategy.

title: Global landscape and emerging trends in programmable mRNA-based therapeutics for myocardial infarction: a multi-database bibliometric analysis.
abstract: Myocardial infarction (MI) remains a leading cause of mortality worldwide. Although current reperfusion-based interventions have significantly improved clinical outcomes, they are insufficient to restore lost cardiomyocytes or repair irreversible myocardial injury. Programmable messenger RNA (mRNA)-based therapeutics have emerged as a cutting-edge strategy for cardiac regenerative repair owing to their advantages of transient and controllable protein expression, high design flexibility, and avoidance of genomic integration. However, the global research landscape, collaborative networks, and evolving scientific priorities in this rapidly expanding field have not yet been systematically characterized. A comprehensive bibliometric analysis was conducted using publications retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and PubMed databases from 2012 to 2026. After literature screening and deduplication, 814 publications from WoSCC and 4,155 publications from PubMed were included. VOSviewer, CiteSpace, and the R package Bibliometrix were used to conduct parallel analyses of annual publication trends, country- and institutional-collaboration networks, journal and author distributions, reference citation bursts, and keyword-based thematic evolution. WoSCC analysis revealed a fluctuating but overall increasing publication trajectory, with annual research output peaking at ∼90 publications in 2023. The evolution of this field could be categorized into three stages: an emerging phase (2012-2016), a developmental phase (2017-2021), and an accelerated expansion phase (2022 onward). China and the United States represented the leading contributors, while institutions including Harvard University and the Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences-Peking Union Medical College served as major research hubs. Circulation Research and Circulation occupied central positions within the co-citation network. ZANG, LICHUN was identified as the most productive author, whereas the landmark 2013 study by Zangi L represented the most influential foundational contribution to the field. Parallel analysis of PubMed further validated the identified evolutionary trends and highlighted angiogenesis as a promising yet underexplored research direction. Research on programmable mRNA therapeutics for MI is rapidly expanding, with the focus shifting from fundamental molecular mechanisms to translational applications that enable precise inflammatory modulation, fibrosis reversal, and revascularization. Future breakthroughs will likely depend on the development of efficient and cardiac-targeted delivery platforms, as well as deeper exploration of epitranscriptomic therapeutic strategies, to accelerate clinical translation.

title: Mapping high resolution, multidimensional phase diagrams of near-physiological protein condensates.
abstract: Biomolecular condensates are membraneless compartments, crucial for organising and regulating diverse cellular processes. Current approaches to study condensate biology either use simplified recombinant protein systems with limited physiological relevance, or complex live-cell models with restricted experimental control and scalability. Here, we present ExVivo PhaseScan, a droplet microfluidics platform that couples mammalian lysate-based reconstitution with scalable analysis to generate high-resolution phase diagrams of compositionally complex protein condensates. We apply this approach to study two multicomponent condensate systems, stress granules and nucleoli, and dissect the physicochemical interactions that influence their stability. We further developed a machine learning pipeline to analyse condensate morphology which we use to reveal how mutations in the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)-linked protein Fused in Sarcoma (FUS) remodels condensate properties. We identify liquid-to-solid transitions of mutant FUS within stress granules and nucleoli, and show that these transitions can be reversed by RNA aptamer-based interventions. Together, these findings establish ExVivo PhaseScan as a versatile tool for dissecting the physicochemical and pathological regulation of condensates, with potential to inform therapeutic strategies for diseases driven by aberrant phase transitions.

title: AI-Driven Design of Next-Generation Immunoinformatics Multi-Epitope Subunit Vaccine Targeting the Most Virulent Mpox Proteome: A Structural and Kinetic Validation Framework
abstract: The resurgence of the Mpox virus (MPXV) highlights the urgent need for scalable, mutation-resistant countermeasures. Slow development timelines hinder traditional empirical vaccine discovery, while conventional vaccinology often yields high false-positive rates because it relies on static, linear sequence-based screening. These classical informatics filters consistently fail to predict physical structural stability or the dynamic presentation of immune cells under physiological conditions, creating a distinct translational gap between computational design and in vitro efficacy. To address these limitations, here we engineered an advanced, AI-augmented vaccine discovery pipeline targeting the most virulent components of the MPXV proteome. We systematically screened eight critical viral targets essential for replication, membrane morphogenesis, and host-cell entry to map highly conserved T-cell and B-cell epitopes. Moving beyond standard heuristic filtering, we implemented a high-fidelity deep learning validation layer: ESM-2 protein language models (pLMs) were deployed to calculate pseudo-perplexity scores across chimeric linker junctions (EAAAK, GPGPG) to guarantee structural naturalness, MHCflurry ensemble models successfully verified active intracellular antigen presentation, and structure-informed graph neural networks (GNNs) simulated the physical node-attention dynamics of the immune synapse. Finally, recurrent neural networks (RNNs)-driven mRNA kinetic modeling optimized translation initiation rates and minimum free energy profiles during in silico cloning. This multi-layered pipeline successfully yielded three structurally refined, multi-epitope vaccine constructs optimized for maximum global population coverage. ESM-2 structural validation confirmed exceptionally low perplexity scores at structural junctions, indicating that the engineered chimaeras have native-like stability and a minimized risk of proteolysis. GNN-based immune synapse modeling demonstrated highly stable binding kinetics and robust binding free energies between the target epitopes and human HLA alleles. Furthermore, RNN kinetic optimizations established that the cDNA sequences are optimized for high-yield expression in heterologous expression hosts without risk of ribosomal stalling or translational bottlenecks. This study establishes a deep learning-augmented framework that bridges the gap between theoretical sequence optimization and biopharmaceutical scalability. By validating the structural naturalness, real-world immunogenicity, and manufacturing kinetics of our vaccine chimeras, this framework presents a robust, proactive paradigm for rapid vaccine architecture against emerging orthopoxvirus threats.

title: Berberine as a Multitarget Therapeutic Agent: Insights from Molecular Docking Studies.
abstract: Natural compounds are crucial in pharmacological research for modulating numerous biological processes. This is particularly helpful in the case of complex diseases and in overcoming challenges (e.g., drug resistance and adverse effects). Berberine, an isoquinoline alkaloid extracted from plants such as Berberis, Coptis, and Hydrastis species, exhibits a wide range of activities, including antidiabetic, anticancer, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and antiviral. However, due to its low oral bioavailability (poor absorption, high first-pass metabolism, along with rapid elimination), further mechanistic understanding and optimization are required. This review brings together molecular docking data to identify berberine's major targets implicated in various diseases, evaluate its multifunctional therapeutic potential, while exploring the benefits, drawbacks, as well as future research avenues of the methodology. A systematic search of databases, including PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar (as of March 2026), was conducted to identify docking studies providing binding affinity and interaction details. Target scores, Protein Data Bank (PDB) IDs, software/scoring functions (e.g., Auto Dock/Vina, Glide, GOLD, Discovery Studio), and validation methods (e.g., redocking, Root-Mean-Square Deviation (RMSD), and important residues that interact with the target were extracted. Berberine showed good predicted affinities at metabolic targets (between -5.4 and -10.5 kcal/mol) with the highest affinities for AKT1 (3O96; -10.5 kcal/mol) and GLUT4 (-10.1 kcal/mol), which included stabilizing contacts such as GLN79, LYS268, and VAL270 in AKT1 and inflammatory mediators such as TNF-α, TYR103, and TRP107 in GLUT4. Antimicrobial docking studies showed good binding to DNA polymerase III (2POL, -5.32 kcal/mol; GLY219) and FtsZ (8GZY, -6.59; FTSZ), notably FTSZ (3VDB, -38.95 kcal/mol; multiple hydrophobic residues). Anticancer targets included BRAF (1UWJ; -9.53) and exceptionally low energies for Aldose Reductase (ADR) (-48.17 kcal/mol; MM-GBSA), phosphodiesterase 4D (-41.58 kcal/mol), Glucocorticoid Receptor (GR) (-37.08), DHODH (-34.81 kcal/mol), and PDK1 (-31.31 kcal/mol), implicating modulation of the MAPK and PI3K/AKT pathways. Antiinflammatory docking found the top binders to be COX-2 (4COX; -10.16 kcal/mol) and PTGS2 (to -9.0 kcal/mol), while antiviral studies identified SARS-CoV-2 Mpro (6LU7; -9.65 kcal/mol; residues including HIS41, CYS145, and GLU166) and other proteins binding to PLpro, RNAdependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), Spike, alongside Dengue proteins. Multitarget complex formation is promoted by recurring hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic, electrostatic, and π-π interactions, all of which are consistent with the planar, positively charged tetracyclic scaffold of berberine (C20H18NO4 +, 336.38 g/mol). There is methodological variation in docking protocols across studies, and the concordance between scores and activities remains inconsistent; however, datasets with identical parameters remain comparable. Overall, docking evidence reveals berberine to be a multitarget, broad-spectrum lead molecule and further supports the necessity of validating the molecule through molecular dynamics studies, experimental trials, clinical trials, and by designing derivatives, using nanotechnology for delivery, with artificial intelligence optimization, and in combination with other drugs to overcome its pharmacokinetic limitations and transform computational results into therapeutic potential.

title: Bioorthogonal Vitamin C Probes Enable Cellular Profiling and Investigation of Lysine Vitcylation.
abstract: Vitamin C is an essential micronutrient, yet its direct chemical engagement with the proteome remains poorly defined. Here, we develop and experimentally benchmark a bioorthogonal probe platform for labeling, profiling, and imaging of lysine vitcylation, a recently identified vitamin C-derived post-translational modification, in living cells. Chemoproteomic analysis and fluorescence imaging reveal a candidate vitcylome enriched in nucleolar proteins associated with ribonucleoprotein biogenesis and RNA processing, and reporter-derived lysine adducts on selected targets were validated by mass spectrometry. Time-resolved analyses demonstrate that intracellular vitcylation undergoes unexpectedly rapid remodeling, indicating active cellular regulation. Furthermore, a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen identifies glutathione S-transferase P1 (GSTP1) as an upstream regulator of global vitamin C-derived protein modification, linking vitcylation remodeling to cellular electrophile handling and redox homeostasis. Collectively, this platform provides a chemical framework for profiling, visualizing, and investigating protein vitcylation in living cells, and reveals vitcylation as a dynamic, spatially organized and regulated metabolic modification.

title: The novel regulatory influence of Argonaute 1 on messenger RNA 5-methylcytosine modification in Arabidopsis thaliana.
abstract: 5-Methylcytidine (m5C) modifications play a critical role in RNA metabolism. TRM4B (tRNA-specific methytransferase 4B) is the only known component of the plant m5C machinery that mediates mRNA (messenger RNA) methylation. To date, no regulators governing site-specific m5C modifications have been identified, apart from several degenerated sequence motifs. Drawing on relevant findings in animals, we investigated the involvement of AGO1 (Argonaute 1) in m5C regulation using an ago1 mutant of Arabidopsis. m5C-RIP-seq (m5C RNA immunoprecipitation followed by deep sequencing) identified high-confidence 5981 and 4559 m5C peaks in WT (wild type) and ago1, respectively. A substantial proportion of these peaks overlapped between WT and ago1, indicating their high gene specificity. Compared to WT, ago1 exhibited 366 hyper-methylated and 168 hypo-methylated peaks. While both hyper- and hypo-methylation could correlate with either up- or down-regulated gene expression, actively transcribed genes with relatively complex structures were preferentially targeted by m5C modification. A significant fraction of m5C-associated genes are functionally involved in mRNA surveillance and ribosome biogenesis. Intriguingly, over 60% of m5C peaks identified in WT were associated with the miRNA (microRNA) binding sites. Furthermore, AGO1 binding signals could be detected on the corresponding transcripts for >40% of the m5C peaks based on the AGO1-RIP-seq experiment. Immunoprecipitation coupled to mass spectrometry validated the interaction between TRM4B and TRANSPORTIN1 (TRN1)-a known AGO1-interacting protein that is also implicated in the miRNA pathway. These findings support a model in which the miRNA-guided AGO1 complex plays a critical role in mediating site-specific m5C modifications.

title: Cardiac fibroblast deletion of PTBP1 modulates the profibrotic response by alternative splicing.
abstract: Dynamic cardiac fibroblast phenotypes drive pathological remodeling and fibrosis, yet post-transcriptional mechanisms controlling fibroblast activation remain poorly defined. Here, we identify the RNA-binding protein polypyrimidine tract binding protein 1 (PTBP1) as a regulator of cardiac fibroblast activation and fibrotic remodeling. Cardiac fibroblast-specific Ptbp1 deletion reduced fibrosis and preserved cardiac function after Angiotensin II infusion, transverse aortic constriction, and myocardial infarction. In vitro, PTBP1 depletion attenuated TGFβ-induced myofibroblast activation, decreasing αSMA and POSTN expression and impairing collagen gel contraction. Transcriptomic and splicing analyses revealed broad PTBP1-dependent gene expression and alternative splicing programs enriched for extracellular matrix organization, cytoskeletal remodeling, and fibroblast function. Mechanistically, PTBP1 regulated Fgfr1 alternative splicing, and restoration of the FGFR1β isoform partially rescued the contractile defect caused by PTBP1 loss. Together, these findings establish PTBP1-dependent alternative splicing as a key mechanism promoting cardiac fibroblast activation and pathological fibrosis.

title: Antiviral immunity via telomerase-like reverse transcription in bacteria.
abstract: Defense-associated reverse transcriptases (DRTs) employ diverse and distinctive mechanisms of cDNA synthesis to protect bacteria against viral infection1. However, the functions and mechanisms of many DRTs remain unknown2. Here we identify a new antiviral defense system, DRT10, that associates with a noncoding RNA (ncRNA) to catalyze processive, protein-primed synthesis of tandem-repeat DNA. Reverse transcription is templated by a defined ncRNA region with a characteristic sequence pattern and template boundary elements, both of which are conserved and essential for DNA repeat addition. Cryo-EM reconstructions reveal an unanticipated 2:1 architecture, wherein two RT monomers bind opposite sides of a pseudo-symmetric ncRNA. Biochemical experiments further demonstrate that each RT monomer reverse transcribes the template encoded on its respective side of the ncRNA, but only one generates the long repetitive product, whose template is defined by the distance between two flanking stem-loop anchors. This mode of iterative, boundary-delimited cDNA synthesis exhibits direct parallels to the mechanism of telomeric repeat addition by eukaryotic telomerase, and phylogenetic analyses of RTs across domains of life place telomerase in a monophyletic clade with the DRT family, suggesting a common origin for their DNA polymerization activities. Together with earlier studies of DRT2, DRT3, and DRT93-5, our findings identify a conserved mechanistic logic underlying RNA-templated DNA repeat addition across diverse DRTs, despite vastly different architectural solutions, and expand the repertoire of reverse transcription-based strategies for antiviral immunity in bacteria.

title: Targeting the H3K4me3-HNRNPC-CD24 Axis Overcomes Stemness and Immunosuppression in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is driven by cancer stemness and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, which collectively contribute to therapeutic resistance. While the RNA-binding protein HNRNPC has been implicated in tumor progression, it has primarily been characterized as a downstream effector, and its autonomous regulatory functions, particularly in governing cancer stemness, remain entirely unexplored. Through multi-omics analyses of HCC cohorts, we identified HNRNPC as a pivotal driver of a high-risk molecular subtype. Mechanistically, HNRNPC expression was transcriptionally activated via WDR5/KMT2A complex-mediated deposition of H3K4me3 at its promoter. Functionally, HNRNPC was essential for maintaining cancer stemness, promoting tumor growth and metastasis, and conferring oxaliplatin resistance. Notably, depletion of HNRNPC reprogrammed the immunosuppressive microenvironment by enhancing CD8+ T cell infiltration, reducing T cell exhaustion, and polarizing macrophages toward an M1-like anti-tumor phenotype. At the molecular level, HNRNPC bound to the m6A-modified 3'UTR of CD24 mRNA in an RNP2 motif-dependent manner, thereby enhancing its stability and elevating CD24 protein expression. Therapeutically, we developed a novel lipid nanoparticle (LNP) encapsulating siRNA against HNRNPC. Systemically administered AP-EG-si potently suppressed tumor growth, attenuated stemness, and synergized with anti-PD-L1 therapy to enhance anti-tumor immunity. Our findings thus unveil the H3K4me3-HNRNPC-CD24 axis as a central epigenetic and post-transcriptional regulatory pathway that coordinately drives HCC stemness and immune evasion, nominating HNRNPC-targeted nanotherapy as a promising strategy for advanced HCC.

title: A comparative analysis of cell death signalling in RNA and DNA virus infections and potential inhibitory strategies.
abstract: The recent COVID-19 pandemic and the epidemic outbreak of Mpox have demonstrated that viruses, despite their apparently simple structure, are sophisticated microorganisms that have evolved complicated pro-survival mechanisms. Their potential to manipulate cell death pathways can affect and determine the outcome of the infection cycle and the host's immune response. RNA viruses typically display a more acute and aggressive nature, as they often promote cell death. In this way, they proliferate and release their virions to infect adjacent cells and perpetuate their life cycle. Common consequences of RNA virus infection include hyperinflammatory responses in hosts, typically leading in damage to the epithelial barrier. Conversely, DNA viruses modulate these pathways to sustain a balance between the lytic cycle, during which they replicate, and latency, wherein they remain inactive until an appropriate stimulus triggers reactivation. Achieving this balance and transitioning between stages of infection requires the inhibition of cellular death processes. In both instances, the viruses seem to respond to the cellular context, enhancing their adaptability through mutations, so to deceive host defenses and therefore secure their survival. This highlights the necessity to comprehend the processes via which these biological threats induce cell death, thereby facilitating the development of broad-spectrum or targeted antiviral treatments.

title: Revisiting mRNA capping in Mononegavirales: a promising, yet underexplored antiviral target.
abstract: mRNA capping is a co-transcriptional, nuclear process in eukaryotes that adds a cap onto the 5' end of RNA to confer stability, efficient translation, and nuclear export. Viruses have evolved diverse strategies by mimicking or subverting host pathways to install an mRNA cap for efficient gene expression and evasion of the host innate immune response. The conventional mRNA capping pathway, employed by many RNA and DNA viruses, is mediated by dedicated RNA 5'-triphosphatase, guanylyltransferase, and methyltransferase enzymes. In contrast, many RNA viruses utilize unconventional capping mechanisms that diverge from the canonical pathway, offering unique opportunities to develop virus family-specific antiviral therapeutics. Among negative-sense RNA viruses, members of the order Mononegavirales harbor a unique capping domain, polyribonucleotidyltransferase (PRNTase), embedded within the viral RdRp large (L) protein. Unlike the conventional guanylyltransferase-mediated mechanism, PRNTase catalyzes mRNA capping through the formation of a covalent L-pRNA intermediate rather than the canonical GMP-enzyme intermediate. The HR motif in PRNTase, involved in covalent linking to mRNA, is highly conserved in non-segmented negative-strand RNA viruses. This review focuses on structural and functional insights into Mononegavirales capping, highlighting the conserved motifs and domain architecture that make it a promising therapeutic target.

title: Molecular basis for developing tumor-targeted siRnas for future immunotherapy.
abstract: Certain immune signaling pathways contribute to cancer progression by promoting tumor immune evasion through immune checkpoint activation, immunosuppressive cytokine production, metabolic depletion, and altered intracellular signaling. Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) provide a programmable strategy for selectively silencing genes involved in immunosuppression, offering a targeted approach to enhance antitumor immunity. This review highlights the rationale for targeting immune regulatory factors with siRNA in cancer immunotherapy. Key targets include immune checkpoints (e.g. programmed cell death protein 1 and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4), immunosuppressive mediators (e.g. transforming growth factor beta 1 and indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1), and intracellular regulators (e.g. suppressor of cytokine signaling 1 and signal transducer and activator of transcription 3). Preclinical and early clinical studies show that silencing these targets restores T-cell activity, improves antigen presentation, remodels the tumor microenvironment, and enhances anti-tumor immunity. Additionally, advances in siRNA delivery methods are accelerating clinical translation. By silencing genes involved in immune suppression, siRNAs can restore T cell activation and improve the efficacy of cancer vaccines and adoptive cell therapies. However, significant challenges remain, including achieving efficient cell-specific delivery and minimizing off-target effects.

title: ZBP1 specifically binds pre-formed Z-RNA, limiting its potential pool of nucleic acid ligands compared to ADAR1.
abstract: ZBP1 senses foreign nucleic acids in the unusual, left-handed Z-conformation via binding through its Zα1 and Zα2 domains and initiates cell death pathways that enable viral clearance. dsDNA and dsRNA can adopt Z-conformations; however, both typically require chemical modifications or protein binding to induce Z-form conversion and stabilization. ZBP1 has been previously shown to bind and convert B-DNA to the Z-conformation and was assumed to be able to convert A-RNA as well, despite the lack of experimental validation. Here, we use NMR and other biophysical and biochemical experiments to characterize the Z-DNA and Z-RNA binding properties of ZBP1's Zα1 and Zα2 domains. While ZBP1's Zα domains are able to convert and stabilize unmodified dsDNA in the Z-conformation, they are incapable of flipping unmodified (CpG)n repeat dsRNA. ZBP1's Zα domains require dsRNAs with Z-promoting chemical modifications to be able to bind and stabilize the Z-conformation. These results contrast with ADAR1's Zα domain, which can bind and flip both dsDNA and dsRNA into the Z-conformation, potentially indicating finely tuned competition between ADAR1 and ZBP1 for pro-survival and pro-death outcomes, respectively. This work highlights the functional variability of Zα domains and narrows down potential physiological substrates of ZBP1 in infection and disease.

title: PXL: a nucleic acid-binding module of the promyelocytic leukemia protein.
abstract: The promyelocytic leukemia protein (PML) is a stress-response factor that assembles into PML nuclear bodies, dynamic subnuclear compartments involved in tumor suppression and antiviral defense. The most abundant isoform, PML-1, has been linked to transcriptional regulation, genome stability, and antiviral responses, yet the molecular basis of these functions remains unclear and is generally attributed to proteins associated with PML nuclear bodies. Here, we report that PML-1 itself harbors a previously structurally uncharacterized nucleic acid-binding domain. The domain, termed PXL, is encoded by exon 9 of the PML gene and is unique to isoform 1. Its structure reveals an exonuclease III fold, but lacks the catalytic residues required for activity, defining PXL as a pseudo-exonuclease. Biochemical, structural, mutational, and cellular analyses demonstrate that PXL specifically binds G-rich oligonucleotides implicated in G-quadruplex formation and displays a strong in vitro preference for polyUG RNA. Furthermore, deletion of the PXL domain significantly decreases PML colocalization with G-quadruplexes in cells, downregulates genomic maintenance pathways, and modulates the expression of E2F target and interferon-α response genes. These findings provide a molecular basis for previous observations implicating PML in nucleic acid-associated functions and establish a mechanistic framework for future studies of PML-mediated stress responses, nuclear organization, and gene regulation.

title: FTO-Mediated m6A Demethylation in Insulin Resistance and Type 2 Diabetes: Tissue-Specific Mechanisms - a Narrative Review.
abstract: This narrative review aims to clarify the tissue-specific effects of the fat mass and obesity-associated (FTO) gene, which encodes a demethylase enzyme, on lipid and glucose metabolism and appetite regulation. Some FTO single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) regulate neighboring genes, while the FTO protein demethylates single-stranded nucleic acids. The FTO enzyme modulates RNA lifecycle processes, including splicing, export, decay, and translation. However, recent studies suggest that FTO expression and activity may influence metabolic signals across multiple tissues. Evidence from genetic-association studies, experimental cellular and animal models, and human metabolic studies suggests tissue-specific effects of FTO, although findings are not always consistent across evidence types. In the liver, FTO has been reported to promote lipogenesis through effects on SREBP-1c maturation and the expression of lipogenic genes. In adipocytes, FTO has been implicated in adipogenesis through effects on Mitotic Clonal Expansion (MCE), including regulation of RUNX1T1 splicing, during terminal differentiation through effects on C/EBP-β transcription. In addition to effects attributed to FTO protein, the FTO locus-mediated mechanisms can influence neighboring genes such as IRX3, which has been implicated in adipocyte thermogenic programs. FTO has also been implicated in the regulation of gluconeogenic gene expression in the liver. In skeletal muscle, FTO has been associated with altered AMPK signaling and lipid accumulation. In pancreatic β-cells, FTO has been reported to affect insulin secretion, although findings are inconsistent across experimental models. In the hypothalamus, FTO-related mechanisms have been linked to RPGRIP1L and leptin signaling, suggesting a potential role in appetite regulation. FTO inhibitors have also been investigated for their potential to modulate FTO-related effects. In summary, FTO dysregulation may be involved in insulin resistance and metabolic risk factors associated with T2D. However, the underlying mechanisms and causal relationships remain incompletely established, particularly given differences among genetic-association studies, experimental models, and human metabolic studies.

title: Advances in plant metabolic engineering through synthetic biology.
abstract: The challenges associated with the escalating global population and climate change in crop production and food security are substantial. This underscores the necessity for improvements in crop nutrition, yield, and resilience to environmental stresses. Plant metabolic pathways directly influence growth, nutrient accumulation, and stress responses, rendering them prime targets for crop enhancement. Advances in plant synthetic biology and gene editing are facilitating more precise modifications of genes, regulatory elements, and metabolic pathways. This review highlights the primary technologies used in plant metabolic engineering and focuses on representative examples of their implementation for crop improvement, including but not limited to CRISPR-Cas systems, multiplex genome editing, knock-in and knock-out strategies, CRISPR-mediated gene regulation (CRISPRi/CRISPRa), base editing, prime editing, RNA targeting technologies, synthetic promoters, and gene stacking strategies. Furthermore, the emerging role of artificial intelligence in the design and optimization of metabolic pathways and genome editing tools will be briefly discussed.

title: CD98hc marks a precursor of human stem cell-derived alpha cells primed for functional maturation.
abstract: Pluripotent stem cell-derived alpha cells (SC-α cells) represent a promising component of next-generation cell therapies designed to more fully recapitulate human islet function; however, heterogeneity and the presence of undesired side populations limit their functional maturity and therapeutic potential. Here, we identify the cell surface protein CD98hc (SLC3A2), that when highly expressed in precursor cells, is associated with differentiation toward a more transcriptionally and functionally mature population of human SC-α cells. Directed differentiation was used to generate SC-α cells from pluripotent stem cells, which were assessed via single cell RNA sequencing, flow cytometry, and immunofluorescence imaging. Following magnetic activated cell sorting (MACS) of CD98hc enriched precursors, SC-α cell function was assessed using glucose stimulated glucagon secretion (GSGS). We show that CD98hc is upregulated in SC-α cells expressing high levels of genes known to play important roles in α cell identity and function, and that CD98hc expression is elevated at the pre-α precursor stage relative to non-α cell populations. We demonstrate that magnetic enrichment of CD98hc⁺ pre-α cells derived from multiple pluripotent stem cell lines selectively increases the proportion of the highest CD98hc expressing glucagon-copositive precursors while depleting multiple undesired side populations, including somatostatin-positive and SOX9-positive cells. Although total α cell yield equalizes following complete differentiation, SC-α cells derived from high-CD98hc enriched precursors exhibit significantly enhanced glucose-responsive glucagon secretion compared to sham-sorted controls, indicating improved functional maturation of this precursor population. Together, these findings establish that high expression levels of CD98hc marks a functionally superior α cell precursor, that enrichment at the precursor stage can bias differentiation toward higher functional α cell output, that stem cell-derived α cell populations harbor intrinsic functional heterogeneity, and that selective targeting of precursor populations represents a generalizable strategy to improve the quality and performance of stem cell-derived endocrine cell products.

title: Electrochemical ultrasensitive detection of miRNA-21 via RAFT/ROMP dual polymerization amplification.
abstract: The ultrasensitive detection of microRNAs in bodily fluids is crucial for early diagnosis of cancer. Herein, we design an electrochemical biosensor based on a dual-signal amplification strategy utilizing reversible addition-fragmentation chain transfer (RAFT) and ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP) to achieve ultra-sensitive quantitative detection of miRNA-21. The sensing interface starts from a gold electrode carrying a thiol-immobilized peptide nucleic acid (PNA) capture probe. Once miRNA-21 hybridizes specifically with the PNA, we anchor the RAFT chain-transfer agent 2-(dodecylthiocarbonothioylthio)-2-methylpropionic acid (CDTPA) onto the duplex by taking advantage of Zr4+ coordination chemistry. With the azo initiator 2,2'-azobis[2-(2-imidazolin-2-yl) propane] dihydrochloride (VA-044), in solution, the monomer dicyclopentenyloxyethyl acrylate (DCPEA)-which bears a cyclopentene side group-undergoes RAFT polymerization, decorating the duplex with polymer chains that bristle with pendant cyclopentene rings. Subsequently, the ruthenium-based catalyst AquaMet ((4-((4-ethyl-4-methylpiperazin-1-ium-1-yl)methyl)-1,3-dimesitylimidazolidin-2-ylidene)dichloro(2-isopropoxybenzylidene) ruthenium(II)) chloride coordinates with the cyclopentene groups, catalyzing the ROMP of cyclopentene-based ferrocene (CFc), thereby forming a polymer brush rich in ferrocene electroactive molecules on the electrode surface, achieving efficient two-stage amplification of the electrochemical signal. Under optimized conditions, the sensor returns a linear response to miRNA-21 from 10-17 M to 10-13 M and reaches a detection limit as low as 4.72 aM. Signals from single-mismatched RNA, triple-mismatched RNA, and miRNA-320b were all strongly suppressed relative to the target, while the sensor also proved to be stable in one week and remarkably unfazed by complex biological backgrounds.

title: The orchid Gastrodia-derived extracellular vesicles deliver miR535 to suppress a fungal effector and facilitate symbiosis with Armillaria.
abstract: Plant-derived extracellular vesicles (PDEVs) are nanoscale lipid bilayer structures that facilitate cross-kingdom communication by transporting bioactive molecules, including proteins and small RNAs. While their roles in plant immunity against fungal pathogens are well-established, their functions in beneficial or symbiotic interactions, particularly with mycorrhizal fungi, remain largely unexplored. Here, we investigated the function of PDEVs in the symbiosis between the fully mycoheterotrophic orchid Gastrodia elata and its fungal partner Armillaria gallica. We isolated and characterized G. elata-derived EVs (GeEVs), and confirmed their typical morphology and the presence of the EV marker PEN1. We demonstrated that GeEVs significantly inhibit A. gallica growth and downregulate fungal genes associated with pathogenicity. Small RNA sequencing revealed that GeEVs are rich in specific miRNAs, including gel-miR535, which is undetectable in EVs from model autotrophic plants. Overexpression of gel-miR535 in A. gallica phenocopied the inhibitory effect of GeEV treatment on fungal growth. We further identified that gel-miR535 directly targets the fungal effector gene Ag_07049. Functional assays showed that Ag_07049 is a secreted protein localized to the plant cytoplasm and nucleus. Upon expression in plant cells, it suppresses BAX- and INF1-triggered programmed cell death (PCD), reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, and callose deposition, suggesting that Ag_07049 functions as an immunosuppressive effector. Our findings indicate a novel regulatory mechanism in which a mycoheterotrophic plant utilizes EVs to deliver a miRNA targeting a fungal effector gene, potentially limiting the pathogenic capacity of its symbiotic partner and support balanced mutualism. This work extends the paradigm of cross-kingdom RNAi to beneficial symbiosis and provides critical insights into the molecular dialogue underpinning orchid mycoheterotrophy.

title: The long noncoding RNA MAPKAPK5-AS1 promotes the formation of hepatitis B virus cccDNA by modulating the expression of NABP1.
abstract: Cellular long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) have been shown to participate in diverse biological pathways, including the regulation of virus infections. However, their functions in the hepatitis B virus (HBV) life cycle still need to be explored. Here, we conducted a loss-of-function screen targeting 1779 human lncRNAs and identified 19 lncRNAs associated with HBV infection. One lncRNA, named MAPKAPK5-AS1 (lnc-MAAS), was identified as a host factor required for HBV infection. Our data suggest that lnc-MAAS is involved in the conversion of HBV relaxed circular DNA into covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA). Furthermore, mechanistic experiments revealed that lnc-MAAS affects cccDNA formation by modulating the expression of nucleic acid binding protein 1 (NABP1). Together, our findings shed light on the roles of host lnc-MAAS and NABP1 in HBV cccDNA formation, which may contribute to the development of novel anti-HBV therapeutics.

title: Swimming Exercise Ameliorates Neuropathic Pain and Is Associated with Hippocampal H19, miR-22, and Wnt/β-Catenin Signaling.
abstract: Physical activity is known to ameliorate neuropathic pain (NP); however, the underlying mechanisms, particularly those involving long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) in the hippocampus, remain poorly understood. In this study, we assessed the impact of swimming training on NP in a mouse model of sciatic nerve injury (SNI), with a focus on the lncRNA H19 and its associated signaling pathway. A male C57BL/6 mouse model of SNI was established and randomly divided into five groups: naïve, sham, sham + swim, SNI, and SNI + swim. The swimming groups underwent a 6-week training regimen. Pain thresholds were assessed at multiple time points post-modeling, and hippocampal tissues were collected on day 43 for analysis. Six weeks of swimming training significantly attenuated mechanical hypersensitivity in SNI mice. Compared with the SNI group, swimming training was associated with reduced hippocampal expression of H19, Wnt3a, and β-catenin. Histological analyses using HE and Nissl staining demonstrated improved neuronal morphology and preservation of neuronal structure in the hippocampus following swimming training. In addition, swimming training modulated hippocampal neuroinflammation, as evidenced by decreased levels of IL-6 and TNF-α and increased expression of the IL-10. These findings indicate that swimming training effectively alleviates NP and hippocampal neuroinflammation in SNI mice and is accompanied by coordinated changes in hippocampal H19, miR-22, and Wnt/β-catenin signaling. These associations suggest a potential involvement of H19-related molecular responses in exercise-mediated neuroprotection; however, further mechanistic studies are required to establish causal relationships.

title: Ribosomal protein eL22 contributes to the assembly of 60S ribosomal subunits in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
abstract: Ribosome biogenesis is a highly coordinated pathway that involves the assembly of ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) with ribosomal proteins (r-proteins) to generate functional ribosomal subunits (r-subunits). The Saccharomyces cerevisiae (yeast) large 60S r-subunit consists of three rRNA molecules and 46 r-proteins. The contributions of nearly all r-proteins of the yeast large r-subunit have been characterized; however, a few non-essential proteins remain poorly understood. Although non-essential, human eL22 has been identified as a key player in p53 regulation during ribosomal stress and as a highly mutated target in cancers. Despite this function, the role of eL22 in ribosome maturation is still ill-defined. In this study, we characterized yeast eL22 r-protein, which is encoded by two paralogous genes that exhibit markedly different expression levels. Our results show that eL22 assembles into intermediate nucleolar pre-60S ribosomal particles. Loss of eL22 impairs cell growth and reduces 60S r-subunit accumulation, phenotypes that are exacerbated at low temperatures. Analysis of pre-rRNA processing by pulse-chase labeling, northern blot hybridization, and primer extension reveals a defect in 27S pre-rRNA maturation, specifically at the level of 27SB pre-rRNA processing. Consequently, nuclear export of eL22-deficient pre-60S particles is mildly impaired. Furthermore, we identify genetic interactions between eL22 and neighboring r-proteins, eL38 and eL31. We conclude that eL22 assembly is required for optimal pre-60S maturation during middle nucleolar stages, particularly at low temperatures, a function likely supported by the cooperative action of other r-proteins associated with common elements of 25S rRNA.

title: An OGP binding protein complex-mimicking peptide hydrogel for dental pulp regeneration.
abstract: The regeneration of the dentin-pulp complex remains a critical challenge in oral regenerative medicine. Osteogenic growth peptide (OGP) has garnered significant attention due to its theoretical ability to promote the differentiation of human dental pulp stem cells (hDPSCs). However, its clinical potential is limited by rapid diffusion and susceptibility to enzymatic degradation within the tissue microenvironment. Inspired by the natural OGP-OGP binding protein (OGPBP) system, this study reports an OGPBP complex-mimicking peptide hydrogel (Gel Nap-OGP) for dental pulp regeneration. Gel Nap-OGP is obtained via ultraviolet-triggered co-assembly of two rationally designed peptides: an OGP mimetic peptide Nap-Phe-Phe-Glu-Tyr-Gly-Phe-Gly-Gly-OH (NapFFEOGP(10-14)) and an OGPBP mimetic peptide Nap-Phe-Phe-Glu-Lys(acrylamide)-Lys(acrylamide)-OH (NapFFEK(aa)K(aa)). The resulting hydrogel nanofiber network loads NapFFEOGP(10-14) through dynamic non-covalent interactions, effectively preventing the peptide from enzymatic degradation and facilitating its controlled release. In vitro studies demonstrate that Gel Nap-OGP maintained favorable cytocompatibility without significantly affecting hDPSC proliferation, while enhancing osteogenic/odontogenic differentiation, as indicated by increased expression of RUNX2, ALP, and DSPP. Furthermore, in vivo experiments confirm its excellent biosafety, along with its ability to enhance mineralized tissue formation in an ectopic renal capsule model. RNA sequencing analyses further reveal that Gel Nap-OGP can modulate gene expression programs related to classical osteogenic/odontogenic signaling pathways. We anticipate that this biomimetic peptide hydrogel could be applied for dental pulp regeneration in clinical settings in the future.

title: Pyridobenzothiazolones as non-nucleoside antivirals: From HCV polymerase inhibition to broad-spectrum antiviral agents.
abstract: Pyridobenzothiazolones (PBTZs) are tricyclic compounds originally investigated as chemotypes directed against viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerases. Following the first reports on hepatitis C virus (HCV) NS5B inhibition, medicinal chemistry optimization and mechanistic studies have expanded the antiviral profile of this scaffold to the inhibition of flaviviruses (including Dengue, Zika, West Nile viruses) and, most recently, of respiratory RNA viruses including human coronaviruses, respiratory syncytial viruses and influenza viruses. This review summarizes the PBTZ chemical series, covering structure-activity relationships, proposed mechanisms of action, antiviral potency ranges, pharmacological limitations, and prospects for clinical development. The available evidence supports PBTZs as a chemically versatile platform capable of engaging both viral enzymes and virion-associated processes, positioning this scaffold as a promising platform for next-generation broad-spectrum antiviral therapeutics.

title: Retinal organoid-based evaluation of icariin-loaded extracellular vesicles for hypoxia-induced retinal injury via mitochondrial modulation.
abstract: Hypoxic injury is a critical pathological factor in various retinal degenerative diseases, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and irreversible loss of retinal neurons. This study investigated the neuroprotective potential of Icariin-loaded extracellular vesicles (EV_ICA) using both R28 retinal progenitor cells and human embryonic stem cell (hESC)-derived retinal organoids. EV_ICA were isolated and characterized by morphology, EV marker expression, and zeta potential analysis. A CoCl2-induced hypoxic injury model was established in R28 cells and hESC-derived retinal organoids to evaluate the therapeutic effects of EV_ICA. Gene and protein expression analyses, bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq), gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), mitochondrial ROS measurements, and intracellular ATP assays were performed to assess neuroprotective efficacy and mitochondrial function. EV_ICA exhibited typical spherical morphology, expressed standard EV markers, and showed a shift toward a less negative zeta potential compared to Naïve EV. In hypoxia-injured retinal models, EV_ICA significantly restored the expression of key retinal and neuroprotective markers, including Syntaxin12, NeuN, Vegf, Rbpms, Brn-3a, and Bdnf, while suppressing Hif-1α accumulation. Transcriptomic and GSEA analyses revealed that EV_ICA reactivated biological pathways associated with phototransduction, visual perception, and retinal development that were impaired under hypoxic conditions. Furthermore, EV_ICA improved mitochondrial homeostasis by up-regulating mitochondrial-related genes, reducing mitochondrial ROS accumulation, and recovering intracellular ATP production. These findings demonstrate that EV_ICA exerts neuroprotective effects by preserving mitochondrial quality control and restoring functional retinal gene programs under hypoxic stress. EV_ICA may therefore serve as a promising therapeutic candidate for hypoxia-related retinal degeneration and provide potential applications for cell-free regenerative medicine.

title: TMEM39A acts as a novel profibrotic factor to activate hepatic stellate cells partially via the cell adhesion molecule signaling axis.
abstract: Hepatic stellate cell (HSC) transdifferentiation into myofibroblasts is a pivotal event in liver fibrosis, yet the underlying regulatory network remains elusive. This study explores the role of TMEM39A in HSC activation and its pro-fibrotic effects via the cell adhesion molecule (CAM) signaling axis. An in vitro HSC activation model was established using TGF-β1-stimulated LX-2 cells, combined with TMEM39A knockdown and overexpression. Cell viability, migration, and apoptosis were assessed by CCK-8, wound healing, Transwell, and flow cytometry. Fibrotic marker expression was measured at both mRNA and protein levels. RNA sequencing and bioinformatics identified the CAM pathway as a candidate downstream effector, and its pharmacological inhibitor (Alicaforsen, an ICAM-1 antagonist) was used for validation. TMEM39A expression correlated positively with HSC activation. Overexpression of TMEM39A promoted LX-2 viability, migration, and upregulation of fibrotic markers (α-SMA, COL1A1) while suppressing apoptosis, whereas knockdown reversed these effects. Mechanistically, TMEM39A activated the CAM axis with specific ICAM-1 elevation. Alicaforsen treatment partially inhibited the activation of HSCs and the expression of fibrosis markers induced by TMEM39A. TMEM39A functions as a novel pro-fibrotic facilitator that promotes HSC activation at least partially through the CAM/ICAM-1 signaling axis. Our findings provide mechanistic insights into liver fibrosis and suggest TMEM39A and its downstream effectors as potential candidates for further therapeutic exploration, pending rigorous in vivo and clinical validation.

title: Senomorphic miR-3155b suppresses the senescence-associated secretory phenotype in therapy-induced senescence.
abstract: Senomorphic microRNAs (miRNAs) are a class of small regulatory RNAs that selectively suppress the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) without eliminating senescent cells, thereby offering a targeted approach to counteract the pro-tumorigenic consequences of therapy-induced senescence (TIS). Despite their therapeutic potential, senomorphic miRNAs in luminal breast cancer remain poorly characterized. Here, we performed small RNA sequencing to profile miRNA expression changes in a doxorubicin-induced TIS model using the luminal breast cancer line MCF7. We identified miR-3155b as a previously uncharacterized miRNA significantly downregulated during TIS. Functional studies revealed that miR-3155b overexpression suppressed the mRNA and protein levels of multiple SASP factors, including IL6, IL8 (CXCL8), MMP13, TNF, IL1B, and IFNB1, whereas its knockdown enhanced their expression. Critically, these effects occurred without affecting core senescence phenotypes such as proliferation arrest, SA-β-gal activity, or DNA damage foci formation. This senomorphic function was further confirmed in an ionizing radiation (IR)-induced TIS model and in T47D luminal breast cancer cells. miR-3155b was confirmed to target the CXCL8 mRNA by luciferase reporter assays, and RNA pull-down assays indicated that miR-3155b physically associates with IFNB1, IL6, TNF, and MMP13 mRNAs. Collectively, our findings identify miR-3155b as a senomorphic miRNA in Luminal A breast cancer TIS and provide a potential target for optimizing chemoradiotherapy strategies aimed at mitigating SASP-driven adverse effects.

title: Akabane virus reprograms the PKR-eIf2α-SGs/PBs axis to fine-tune cap-snatching efficiency.
abstract: Akabane virus (AKAV) initiates transcription in the cytoplasm via the cap-snatching mechanism. Cytoplasmic host mRNAs act as the primary cap donors, whereas the impact of their subcellular localization on the cap-snatching process remains unclear. Herein, we demonstrate that the AKAV-induced disassembly of polysomes, stress granules (SGs), and processing bodies (PBs) collectively facilitates viral cap-snatching. Mechanistically, AKAV infection activates the PKR-eIF2α signaling axis, leading to the disassembly of polysomes and subsequent translational shutoff. Intriguingly, the viral N protein disassembles SGs and PBs by competing for sequestered RNAs within these granules, whereas mutations of its RNA-binding residues abolish this activity. Moreover, PKR-eIF2α inhibition impairs AKAV replication and cap-snatching efficacy. Whereas, inhibition of SGs via G3BP1 knockdown or chemical agents significantly enhances viral replication and cap-snatching efficiency, indicating that polysomes and SGs disassembly favor caps acquisition. Additionally, N protein-mediated PBs disassembly protects mRNA from degradation, and PBs inhibition enhances cap-snatching. Taken together, AKAV has evolved a sophisticated strategy to reprogram mRNA distribution to create an optimal cellular environment for viral cap-snatching.

title: The SGLT2 Inhibitor Empagliflozin Directly Binds Cardiac JNK3, Uncouples c-Jun/c-Fos Signaling, and Confers Cardioprotection in Diabetic Cardiomyopathy.
abstract: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, including empagliflozin (EMPA), confer significant cardioprotection in type 2 diabetes in addition to lowering glucose levels. However, their direct targets in cardiac tissue and molecular mechanisms underlying their effects in diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM) remain unclear. The aim of the present study was to identify a direct cardiac target of EMPA and define the downstream signaling mechanisms mediating its cardioprotective effects in DCM. A kinase activity screening of 107 kinases was used to identify candidate targets for EMPA, followed by protein-ligand docking and surface plasmon resonance to validate direct binding to c-Jun N-terminal kinase 3 (JNK3). The cardioprotective effects of EMPA (10 mg/kg/day, 10 weeks) were evaluated in male db/db mice. Mechanistic studies were performed using AC16 cardiomyocytes under high glucose and palmitic acid (HG/PA) conditions. JNK3 function was examined using pharmacological inhibition with SR-3576, overexpression, and small interfering RNA knockdown. EMPA improved systolic and diastolic function, reduced cardiac fibrosis and mitochondrial injury in db/db mice, accompanied by suppression of c-Jun/c-Fos signaling. Docking and binding analyses demonstrated selective interaction between EMPA and JNK3 over JNK1/2. EMPA inhibited JNK3-dependent c-Jun/c-Fos signaling without altering pan-JNK phosphorylation, indicating selective disruption of JNK3-c-Jun coupling. In AC16 cells, EMPA or JNK3 inhibition reduced c-Jun phosphorylation and restored mitochondrial function. JNK3 overexpression impaired mitochondrial function. EMPA reversed these effects, whereas JNK3 knockdown improved mitochondrial function independently of EMPA treatment. EMPA directly targets JNK3, selectively uncoupling it from c-Jun/c-Fos signaling and thus preserving mitochondrial function and limiting fibrosis in DCM. These findings identify JNK3 as a novel direct target of EMPA in the heart and provide a mechanistic basis to explain the cardioprotective effect of SGLT2 inhibitors.

title: Gpr84 activation induces anti-mycobacterial defense in macrophages via MAPK signaling.
abstract: Tuberculosis (TB), a disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), remains a significant global health threat. The complete pathogenesis of Mtb infection within the host remains insufficiently elucidated, highlighting the urgent need for research focused on host-directed therapeutic strategies targeting infected immune cells. G protein-coupled receptor 84 (Gpr84), an inflammatory receptor expressed on the surface of immune cells, is known to induce inflammatory responses upon activation. We hypothesized that Gpr84 plays a pivotal role in regulating the macrophage response to Mtb infection. In this study, we investigated the role of Gpr84 in controlling intracellular Mtb survival within macrophages. Genetic knockdown of Gpr84 using small interfering RNA (siRNA) significantly increased the Mtb burden. Conversely, treating Mtb-infected macrophages with the Gpr84 agonist 6-n-octylaminouracil (6-OAU) led to a pronounced, dose-dependent reduction in bacterial load. Mechanistically, Gpr84 activation enhanced the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and robustly increased the activation of the MAPK pathway (Erk and Jnk), suggesting a direct mechanism for bacterial clearance. Our findings define Gpr84 as a critical component of host anti-mycobacterial defense, inhibiting Mtb growth in macrophages via the MAPK signaling cascade. This study strongly identifies Gpr84 as a promising host-directed therapeutic target for combating drug-resistant TB.

title: Cell-resolved spatial mapping of antibody-drug conjugate targets in breast cancer.
abstract: Antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) activity and target-dependent on-target/off-tumor toxicity depends in part on which cells express the target antigen, a feature that bulk assays cannot resolve. We analyzed a publicly available whole-transcriptome CosMx breast tumor dataset including 154,816 cells and 18,934 genes. Eleven clinically relevant ADC targets were profiled across seven annotated lineages. Findings were contextualized using TCGA-BRCA bulk transcriptomes (1,097 tumors and 114 normal tissues) and assessed in two public Xenium breast cancer specimens. HER2 (ERBB2), TROP2 (TACSTD2), HER3 (ERBB3), NECTIN4 and MUC1 were enriched in tumor epithelium. B7-H3 (CD276) was highest in endothelial and myoepithelial cells, with similar mean expression in stromal and tumor cells. PSMA (FOLH1) was enriched in endothelium. TCGA-BRCA tumor-normal differences did not identify these cellular sources. No overall-survival association remained after multiple-testing correction or covariate adjustment. HER2 and TROP2 tumor enrichment recurred in both Xenium specimens, whereas EGFR was not tumor restricted. Cell-resolved spatial profiling separated ADC targets enriched in tumor epithelium from those expressed in vascular and stromal compartments. B7-H3 and PSMA localization was consistent with prior immunohistochemical reports and is confirmatory. These RNA-level results do not establish surface-protein abundance, ADC response, or clinical toxicity. Low-abundance microenvironmental findings remain based on a single discovery specimen and require protein-level validation. Protein-level confirmation, and correlation with ADC efficacy and toxicity, are required before these maps can inform clinical decisions.

title: YY1-NSUN7-m5C-HSPA1B axis drives polycystic ovary syndrome pathogenesis via epigenetic stabilization of HSPA1B mRNA.
abstract: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is the most common endocrine disorder in reproductive-age women. Heat shock 70 kDa protein 1B (HSPA1B) is critical for stress response and inflammation, but its role in PCOS remains unknown. To validate HSPA1B as a key pathogenic gene in PCOS and investigate its regulatory mechanisms. Two PCOS datasets (GSE155489, granulosa cells; GSE54250, whole blood) were analyzed for differentially expressed genes. HSPA1B diagnostic value was assessed by ROC curve. Dihydrotestosterone (DHT)-induced KGN cell and dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA)-induced mouse PCOS models were established. siRNA/adenoviral silencing, overexpression, methylated RNA immunoprecipitation (MeRIP), RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP), chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP), luciferase assay, actinomycin D chase, MTT, flow cytometry, ELISA, and Western blot were used to evaluate HSPA1B effects on granulosa cell function and dissect the YY1-NSUN7-m5C-HSPA1B axis. HSPA1B was identified as a core DEG, upregulated in patient blood and DHT-induced KGN cells (AUC = 0.9273). Silencing HSPA1B reversed DHT-induced injury: restored viability, reduced IL-6/IL-1β, decreased apoptosis, stabilized mitochondrial potential, reduced ROS, and inhibited M1 macrophage polarization (all P < 0.05). In vivo, HSPA1B silencing ameliorated ovarian pathology, corrected sex hormones (restored estradiol [E2], decreased testosterone [T]), and alleviated inflammation (all P < 0.01). Mechanistically, NSUN7 bound HSPA1B mRNA 3' UTR, enhancing stability via m5C methylation; Yin Yang 1 (YY1) activated NOP2/Sun RNA methyltransferase 7 (NSUN7) transcription by promoter binding. Rescue experiments established the YY1-NSUN7-m5C-HSPA1B axis. This study revealed the YY1-NSUN7- m5C -HSPA1B epigenetic axis in PCOS pathogenesis, providing a foundation for HSPA1B-targeted therapy.

title: GenDiMug: a generic inclusive multigraph framework to analyze genomic organizations and -omics data at multiple scales
abstract: After decades of investigation, analyses of genome organization remain challenging. This is because genome descriptions are very information-rich and usually rendered as a linear map of genomic features corresponding to an ordered list of position intervals on a nucleic acid macromolecular backbone. This formalism, while accurate, is not fully optimized to mathematically analyze all genome structural properties, in particular the relations between genomic features, nor to integrate large amounts of -omics data, such as transcriptomes, epigenomes, proteomes, meltomes or chromatin accessibility data, which are increasingly available. We therefore developed GenDiMug, a tool that uses a network representation of the genome as a backbone, providing a natural framework to integrate spatial and ontogenetic relationships between genomic features and multi-omics data. We illustrate how this generic approach can be applied to all sorts of genomes, both to visualize genomic topology at contig and chromosomal scales at base-pair resolution, and to analyze genome positional effects using various graph metrics. Using GenDiMug, we further reveal clumping of genes with similar expression levels in eukaryotic genomes and their possible circadian regulation in a photosynthetic alga.

title: Seumetry: a versatile and comprehensive R toolkit to accelerate high-dimensional flow and mass cytometry data analysis.
abstract: Recent progress in flow and mass cytometry technologies enables the simultaneous measurement of over 50 parameters for an individual cell. The resulting increase in data volume and complexity present challenges for conventional analysis methods, which are based on manual gating, are time-consuming and fail to capture unknown or minor cell populations. Advances in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) technologies have prompted the development of computational analysis tools designed to process and analyze high-dimensional biological data. Building on these advances, we here present Seumetry, a framework that combines flow and mass cytometry data-specific analysis methods with the capabilities of Seurat, a powerful tool for the analysis of scRNAseq data. Seumetry offers methods for advanced quality control, data visualizations, and differential population abundance and protein expression analysis. We tested Seumetry on an in-house generated complex dataset of immune cells from different layers of human intestines, demonstrating that Seumetry accurately identifies distinct immune cell populations. Furthermore, benchmarking against public datasets showed that Seumetry aligns with manual-gated results, further validating its use for high-dimensional flow and mass cytometry data. In summary, Seumetry provides a new scalable framework for the comprehensive analysis of high-dimensional cytometry data with seamless integration into commonly used scRNAseq analysis tools, enabling in-depth analysis methods to facilitate biological interpretations. Seumetry code is available open source under an MIT license and the current version can be viewed and used via Github: https://github.com/imsb-uke/Seumetry; and archived on Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21216681. Flow cytometry data generated for this manuscript is available via Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.11935872. Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

title: The role of mitochondrial DNA and RNA in promoting liver disease pathogenesis.
abstract: Mitochondria are a semi-autonomous organelle due to their unique structural organization and independent genetic system, and they play diverse roles in maintaining cellular homeostasis. The liver is the central metabolic organ and performs myriad functions, including energy production, metabolism, and detoxification. Liver diseases account for approximately two million mortalities per year. Mitochondrial dysfunction and damage are implicated in promoting the pathogenesis of different liver diseases. Mitochondria and mitochondrial nucleic acids, namely, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and mitochondrial RNA (mtRNA), have emerged as regulators of innate immunity. Here, we first review the structural organization of mitochondria and the molecular mechanisms governing mitochondrial biogenesis, replication, and transcription. Next, we describe the mechanistic details by which mitochondrial dysfunction causes the release of mtDNA and mtRNA into the cytosol and extracellular milieu. Some of the mechanisms are through the opening of mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP), voltage-dependent anion channel (VDAC) oligomerization, prohibitin (PHB1/2), mitochondria-derived vesicles (MDV), dysfunction of the mtRNA degradosomes, and senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Cell death pathways such as necrosis, necroptosis, and pyroptosis, in addition to perpetuating inflammation, also release mtDNA and mtRNA into the extracellular milieu. The released mtDNA and mtRNA act as damage associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that engage various cytosolic DNA and RNA sensors and pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) such as cyclic guanosine-monophosphate-adenosine-monophosphate synthase (cGAS), toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9), toll-like receptor 3 (TLR3), Z-DNA-binding protein 1 (ZBP1), NOD-like receptor protein 3 (NLRP3), absent in melanoma 2 (AIM2), retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I), melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 (MDA5), protein kinase R (PKR) and activate different signaling cascades downstream. This review provides a contemporary, comprehensive analysis of the available literature on the roles of mtDNA and mtRNA in liver diseases, including metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic/steatohepatitis (MASLD/MASH), alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD), drug-induced liver injury (DILI), viral hepatitis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Thus, the review highlights the potential of both mtDNA and mtRNA to serve as biomarkers of the pathological conditions of the liver, and the way the mitigation of mitochondrial dysfunction and the release of mtDNA or mtRNA can serve as potential therapeutic targets.

title: Integrated genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic analyses prioritize cadmium-responsive class III peroxidases in Salix variegata.
abstract: Class III peroxidases (PRXs) link apoplastic redox regulation with cell-wall remodeling, yet their coordinated transcript- and protein-level responses to cadmium (Cd) remain poorly resolved in woody plants. We identified 80 high-confidence class III PRX genes in Salix variegata and characterized their genomic organization, evolutionary relationships, protein properties, and predicted regulatory features. Root RNA-seq and data-independent acquisition proteomic datasets from plants exposed to 0 or 100 μM CdCl2 for 10 d were then integrated to prioritize members supported across molecular layers. Segmental and dispersed duplication were the predominant expansion modes, and most SvaPRX proteins showed sequence features compatible with extracellular localization. RNA-seq identified 42 upregulated and two downregulated SvaPRX genes. The DIA dataset comprised 22,883 peptides and 6,068 proteins, with 4,849 proteins quantified in all six samples; biological replicates showed high within-treatment correlations and separation of CK and Cd100 in principal component analysis. Forty SvaPRX proteins were quantified, including 11 upregulated and six downregulated proteins. Cross-layer integration reduced the broad transcript-responsive set to seven concordantly upregulated candidates: SvPRX12, SvPRX23, SvPRX41, SvPRX47, SvPRX61, SvPRX62, and SvPRX66. Targeted qRT-PCR provided additional directional support for Cd-induced expression of SvPRX61 and SvPRX62, with response directions consistent across RNA-seq, proteomic, and qRT-PCR datasets. These results establish a reproducible genome-to-proteome framework for prioritizing Cd-responsive class III peroxidases and identify focused candidates for subsequent biochemical and genetic investigation in woody plants.

title: Interlaboratory comparison of immunoprecipitation-based testing for myositis-specific autoantibodies.
abstract: Myositis-specific autoantibodies (MSAs) are clinically important biomarkers that help classify idiopathic inflammatory myopathies and guide clinical management, but reliable detection remains challenging. Immunoprecipitation (IP) is widely regarded as a reference method for MSA detection in specialist laboratories. However, IP comprises a range of related techniques rather than a single standardised assay, and variability between expert laboratories using different IP-based workflows is not well characterised. Serum samples previously submitted to the Bath Diagnostic Serology Service were distributed to three collaborating reference laboratories. Centres analysed samples using their routine workflows, which included radiolabelled protein IP, RNA-IP, IP-western blotting, IP-mass spectrometry, and supplementary immunoassays. Results were interpreted within each laboratory's diagnostic framework, and interlaboratory concordance of MSA detection and specificity assignment was evaluated. Thirty-two samples were included. Overall concordance across overlap groups ranged from 63-78%. Agreement varied by MSA specificity and methodological scope. Anti-Zo, anti-NXP2 and anti-TIF1γ demonstrated the highest reproducibility, whereas anti-PL-7, anti-Jo-1, anti-EJ, anti-Ha and anti-HMGCR were identified only by isolated laboratories. Differences were consistent with variation in IP method, including antigen source, detection modality and availability of reference sera. Complementary assays played an essential role in anti-MDA5, anti-HMGCR and anti-NXP2 antibody detection. These findings demonstrate that IP-based testing should be considered a framework of expert diagnostic practice rather than a single uniform assay. Greater transparency in laboratory methods and reporting practices may improve interpretation of autoantibody results and support more consistent comparison of MSA results across clinical and research settings.

title: M2 macrophage-derived exosomes and miR-132-3p promote gastric cancer cell aggressiveness and attenuate ferroptosis-related changes.
abstract: This study aimed to explore the correlation between the ability of M2-type tumor-correlated macrophage-derived exosomes (EXOs) to trigger the aggressiveness of gastric cancer (GC) cells and the miR-132-3p expression. EXOs were isolated from the conditioned media of M0 and M2 macrophages and characterized by transmission electron microscopy and Western blotting. miR-132-3p expression was determined by qRT-PCR. HGC-27 cells were divided into the control, miR-132-3p mimic, miR-132-3p inhibitor, M0-EXO, and M2-EXO groups. Cell viability, proliferation, migration, and invasion were assessed using CCK-8, EdU, and Transwell assays. Intracellular GSH, SOD, MDA, and iron levels were measured using colorimetric assays. FTH1, LIFR, and GPX4 expressions were detected by Western blotting. RNA sequencing and bioinformatics analyses were performed to investigate miR-132-3p-mediated transcriptional changes and ferroptosis-related pathways in HGC-27 cells. miR-132-3p was significantly enriched in M2 macrophage-derived exosomes and was highly expressed in GC, with its expression associated with tumor stage, grade, and other clinicopathological features. M2-Exo treatment significantly increased miR-132-3p levels in HGC-27 cells. Both miR-132-3p overexpression and M2-Exo treatment enhanced the proliferation, migration, and invasion of HGC-27 cells, and were accompanied by reduced intracellular iron and MDA levels, increased GSH content and SOD activity, upregulated FTH1 and GPX4 expression, and decreased LIFR expression. In contrast, miR-132-3p inhibition produced largely opposite effects. RNA-seq identified 275 differentially expressed genes following miR-132-3p overexpression, including 216 upregulated and 59 downregulated genes. GO and KEGG analyses revealed significant alterations in biological processes and pathways related to oxygen transport, ATP synthesis, oxidative phosphorylation, thermogenesis, spliceosome function, and endoplasmic reticulum protein processing. Integration of the RNA-seq-derived DEGs with FerrDb identified 12 ferroptosis-related DEGs, including 11 upregulated genes and 1 downregulated gene. qRT-PCR validation showed expression patterns broadly consistent with the RNA-seq results. miR-132-3p expression in the EXOs of M2-type macrophages was significantly elevated, and the EXOs of M2-type macrophages significantly triggered the aggressiveness of GC cells and inhibited ferroptosis in GC cells, which may be resulting from the prevention of ferroptosis through the transport of miR-132-3p; nevertheless, the specific mechanism of action needs to be further elucidated.

title: Viroid-Derived siRNAs: Minimal RNAs Driving Multiscale Perturbations of Host Regulatory Systems.
abstract: Viroids are the simplest known infectious agents, consisting of noncoding circular RNAs that replicate autonomously in plant hosts while inducing profound and systemic alterations in host biology. This apparent paradox positions viroids as powerful models for understanding how RNA molecules encode biological information independently of protein translation. A hallmark of viroid infection is the production of viroid-derived small interfering RNAs (vd-siRNAs) by the host RNA silencing machinery. Here, we propose that vd-siRNAs function not merely as antiviroid byproducts, but as active effectors that translate RNA structural information into gene regulatory activity. Through sequence complementarity and selective incorporation into Argonaute complexes, vd-siRNAs influence host gene expression at multiple levels, including transcript abundance, protein accumulation, epigenetic states, and metabolic pathways. Importantly, their effects extend beyond individual targets and are consistent with broader perturbations of interconnected host regulatory networks, potentially contributing to coordinated transcriptional reprogramming and disease-associated phenotypes. By integrating molecular, transcriptomic, epigenetic, and systems-level evidence, we propose a "structure-to-network" perspective in which viroid RNAs function as minimal informational systems capable of interfacing with complex cellular pathways. Within this context, vd-siRNAs emerge as mechanistic links between RNA architecture and multiscale biological responses. Finally, we discuss how this framework expands our understanding of RNA-mediated regulation and highlights the broader regulatory potential of structured noncoding RNAs.

title: Impact of environmental enrichment and allostatic load induced by repeated mixing on the transcriptome of three porcine brain tissues.
abstract: Environmental enrichment and mixing represent two management procedures in pig production with opposing effects: while environmental enrichment can promote welfare by reducing stress, repeated mixing often induces stress and can negatively impact welfare. Despite their importance in pig husbandry, how these opposing management procedures affect brain function at the molecular level remains poorly understood. This study investigated how environmental enrichment and allostatic load induced by repeated mixing influence gene expression patterns across three porcine brain regions: hypothalamus, prefrontal cortex, and hippocampus. Using RNA sequencing, we analyzed brain tissues from 48 gilts subjected to a 2 × 2 factorial design comparing enrichment conditions (enriched vs. barren) and allostatic load (repeated vs. minimal mixing). While environmental enrichment showed minimal impact on gene expression, allostatic load resulted in 38 differentially expressed genes in the hippocampus, primarily involved in hormone regulation, protein transport, and neuronal activity. Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) identified modules moderately correlated with experimental conditions: six modules in hippocampus associated with allostatic load, and four modules in hypothalamus associated with enrichment. Functional annotation revealed that these modules were primarily enriched in biological processes related to synaptic signaling, neuron development, and metabolic activity. Hub genes from these modules were identified, and turned out not to overlap with differentially expressed genes. Our findings suggest that based on this experimental design, the hippocampus may be particularly responsive to stress-induced transcriptomic changes, while the molecular effects of the environmental enrichment appear more subtle. Overall, this study reveals limited but region-specific transcriptional responses to allostatic load in the porcine brain.

title: Esc2 and Rad57 contribute to RNA polymerase II distribution at highly transcribed genes.
abstract: Transcription by RNA polymerase II (Pol II) must be tightly regulated to maintain gene expression homeostasis, yet how Pol II occupancy is shaped at highly active genes remains incompletely understood. Here, we examine the relationship between the homologous recombination-related factors Esc2 and Rad57 and Pol II distribution in budding yeast. Genome-wide analyses reveal that Esc2 and Rad57 preferentially associate with the gene bodies of highly transcribed housekeeping genes and are linked to a chromatin context that also includes the protein phosphatase Sit4 and its cofactor Rrd1. Loss of Esc2 and Rad57 is accompanied by increased Pol II occupancy within gene bodies, whereas the effect on steady-state RNA abundance is selective rather than uniform. Under the tested anchor-away conditions, acute Rad57 depletion in an esc2Δ background did not fully recapitulate the broader transcriptome imbalance and impaired growth observed after chronic Esc2/Rad57 loss. Together, our findings reveal an association between recombination-related factors and gene-body Pol II occupancy and suggest that Esc2/Rad57 loss is linked to transcription-associated chromatin changes in yeast.

title: Development of a messenger RNA therapy for schizophrenia.
abstract: Few gene-disease associations identified by human genetic studies lead to new drugs that advance to first-in-human trials. Schizophrenia exemplifies this translational gap: thousands of gene-disease associations have been reported, but antipsychotics act via mechanisms introduced in the 1950s.
