To close the gap, clinical research strategies are needed that generalize across genes and diseases. Candidate drug targets were defined as genes linked to schizophrenia by population-based studies. Clinical validation of candidate targets was performed through family-based studies. The molecular effects of clinically validated targets were confirmed by correcting mutations in the neurons from affected family members. For one validated target, a messenger RNA (mRNA) drug was developed, and pre-clinical studies of the drug were performed. Carriers of rare protein-truncating variants (PTVs) in schizophrenia risk genes were identified in 30,813 patients of a US healthcare system. These included two female relatives with a rare PTV in GRIA3, which encodes the GluA3 subunit of the AMPA-type glutamate receptor. Further investigation of the family found an X-linked pattern of inheritance between the PTV and severe mental illness. Correction of the PTV in neurons of affected male family members restored GRIA3 expression. A GRIA3 mRNA drug was developed and in mice was well tolerated, resulted in broad brain expression of GluA3, and rescued behavioral abnormalities in a pharmacologically induced psychosis model (MK-801). Further development toward clinical evaluation of a novel GRIA3 mRNA drug to treat schizophrenia is warranted.

title: 6PPD-Q alters zebrafish neurobehavior by inducing neuroinflammation and inhibiting ERK1/2-CREB-BDNF pathway.
abstract: 6PPD-quinone (6PPD-Q) is the main oxidation product of the tire antioxidant 6PPD, and has received increasing attention due to its widespread presence and toxic effects. However, the neurotoxic effects of 6PPD-Q and its potential mechanisms in adult zebrafish remain insufficiently understood. In this study, zebrafish were exposed to environmental concentrations of 6PPD-Q (5, 10, and 20 μg/L) for 21 days. Behavior, brain histopathology, 5-HT and DA levels, and the expression of their related genes were measured. By network toxicology, molecular docking and brain RNA-seq of 6PPD-Q, the possible molecular mechanisms underlying the neurotoxic effects of 6PPD-Q were investigated and the expression of identified pathway or molecules was determined. 6PPD-Q caused neurobehavioral changes and damaged the brain in zebrafish. The levels of 5-HT and DA in brain were reduced, and their related genes expression was downregulated. Network toxicology and RNA-seq identified 5 potential core molecules targeted by 6PPD-Q and these molecules were significantly enriched in MAPK pathway. 6PPD-Q significantly increased the protein levels of TLR4, TRAF6, and p-p38, as well as the mRNA expression of il-6, il-1β and tnf-α, while decreasing the expression level of il-10. Meanwhile, 6PPD-Q significantly reduced the protein levels of MEK1/2, p-ERK1/2, p-CREB, and BDNF. These findings suggest that 6PPD-Q alters neurobehavior in zebrafish, accompanied by monoamine neurotransmitter disruption, activation of inflammatory signaling and suppression of MEK1/2-ERK1/2-CREB-BDNF pathway, providing new insights into 6PPD-Q neurotoxicity and its mechanism.

title: Fructose metabolic heterogeneity drives vancomycin tolerance in clonal Staphylococcus aureus biofilms.
abstract: Bacterial biofilms are characterized by profound heterogeneity, which is a primary driver of their antibiotic recalcitrance and a major obstacle to clinical infection control. However, how metabolic heterogeneity underpins collective antibiotic tolerance within biofilms remains poorly understood, particularly at single-cell resolution. Here, we apply single-cell RNA sequencing to dissect the response of Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 12600 biofilms to vancomycin. We show that vancomycin induces heterogeneous upregulation of the fructose metabolism genes fruA and fruK, which spatially segregates the biofilm into metabolically active and metabolically reduced subpopulations. Active cells exhibit increased fructose consumption, which fuels peptidoglycan biosynthesis and promotes cell wall thickening, as a mechanism that directly enhances vancomycin tolerance. In contrast, certain metabolically reduced subpopulations potentiate oxidative stress repair programs, representing an alternative survival strategy. In a diabetic mouse model characterized by impaired fructose clearance, elevated systemic fructose levels exacerbate pulmonary S. aureus infection, indicating that fructose utilization may reflect clinically relevant features of host susceptibility. Together, our findings uncover a fundamental link between metabolic heterogeneity and antibiotic tolerance in S. aureus biofilms, opening new avenues for the rational design of anti-biofilm therapeutics.

title: METTL3-mediated m6A methylation of lipopolysaccharide-binding protein exacerbates periodontitis by promoting M1 macrophage polarization.
abstract: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease driven by dysregulated immune responses and is closely associated with macrophage polarization. N6-methyladenosine (m6A) methylation represents the most prevalent RNA modification; however, its role in periodontitis remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the mechanism by which m6A modification regulates macrophage polarization during the progression of periodontitis. A periodontitis mouse model was established by ligature induction. RAW264.7 macrophages were treated with Porphyromonas gingivalis-derived lipopolysaccharide (LPS) to simulate inflammatory conditions in vitro. Micro-computed tomography (micro-CT), hematoxylin-eosin and immunohistochemical staining, quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), immunofluorescence staining, methylated RNA immunoprecipitation (MeRIP), and luciferase reporter assays were used to evaluate alveolar bone loss, macrophage phenotypes, and m6A-dependent regulatory mechanisms. Methyltransferase-like 3 (METTL3) expression was significantly upregulated in periodontitis tissues and in LPS-stimulated macrophages. Knockdown of METTL3 attenuated alveolar bone resorption, reduced pro‑inflammatory M1 markers (tumor necrosis factor-alpha [TNF-α], interleukin-6 [IL-6]), and increased M2 markers (IL-10, arginase-1 [Arg-1]) in mice. In LPS-treated RAW264.7 cells, METTL3 knockdown suppressed M1 polarization markers (CD86, TNF-α, IL-1β) and enhanced M2 markers (CD206, transforming growth factor-beta [TGF-β]). Mechanistically, METTL3 stabilized LPS-binding protein (LBP) mRNA via m6A modification, and overexpression of LBP reversed the METTL3 knockdown-mediated suppression of M1 polarization. RNA immunoprecipitation (RIP) and dual-luciferase assays identified YTHDF1 as the m6A reader responsible for recognizing LBP mRNA. These results indicate that METTL3 promotes periodontitis by enhancing LBP mRNA stability through m6A methylation, thereby driving M1 macrophage polarization. This study identifies the METTL3-LBP-YTHDF1 axis as a key regulator of macrophage-driven inflammation in periodontitis, providing new potential therapeutic targets for modulating immune responses in periodontal disease. Periodontitis is a common chronic inflammatory disease that damages gum tissue and tooth-supporting bones and can lead to tooth loss if untreated. Immune cells called macrophages play a key role here-when they become "pro-inflammatory" (promoting inflammation), the disease worsens. We studied a molecule called methyltransferase-like 3 (METTL3), which is more abundant in periodontitis tissues and inflamed cells. Using mouse models and lab-grown cells, we found that reducing METTL3 levels eased inflammation, protected tooth-supporting bones, and shifted macrophages from pro-inflammatory to anti-inflammatory (a type that helps repair tissue). This happens because METTL3 causes a common chemical change in RNA to stabilize another molecule, lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP), with the help of a protein called YTHDF1. Our findings show that the METTL3-LBP-YTHDF1 pathway drives periodontitis by boosting harmful inflammation, offering a new target for developing treatments to regulate immune responses and improve oral health.

title: TFRC-associated ferroptosis in synovial macrophages promotes inflammatory and fibrotic remodeling in osteoarthritis.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a degenerative joint disease; however, the role of ferroptosis in synovial macrophages remains poorly defined. Here, we integrated single-cell RNA sequencing data from human synovial tissues to systematically characterize cellular heterogeneity and ferroptosis-associated alterations. Nine major cell types were identified, among which synovial macrophages exhibited the highest ferroptosis scores, significantly elevated in OA compared with normal controls. Macrophages with high ferroptosis scores showed pronounced upregulation of genes associated with inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and lipid metabolism, indicating a coordinated state of metabolic reprogramming and inflammatory activation. Using an ensemble machine learning framework, we identified and validated key ferroptosis-related genes, including TFRC, GCLC, GSS, and TP53. Notably, TFRC demonstrated superior specificity and sensitivity and was strongly correlated with ferroptosis activity. Cell-cell communication analysis further revealed that ferroptosis-high macrophages function as central signaling hubs, transmitting TNF- and TGFβ-mediated signals to stromal and vascular cells, thereby promoting synovial inflammation, fibrosis, and angiogenesis. Collectively, our findings identify TFRC as a candidate ferroptosis-associated marker in synovial macrophages and suggest that ferroptosis-associated changes are linked to pro-inflammatory polarization and pathogenic intercellular communication in OA. These findings provide insights into the potential involvement of ferroptosis in synovial macrophage dysfunction and highlight ferroptosis-related pathways as potential therapeutic targets for further investigation.

title: SQSTM1/p62 knockdown induces transcriptomic changes and hepatopancreatic structural alterations in Litopenaeus vannamei.
abstract: SQSTM1/p62 is a multifunctional adaptor protein involved in selective autophagy, oxidative stress regulation and innate immune signaling. However, its role in crustaceans in the absence of an experimental pathogen challenge remains largely unclear. In this study, RNA interference (RNAi) was used to investigate the transcriptional consequences of Lv-p62 knockdown in the hepatopancreas of Litopenaeus vannamei. Transcriptomic analysis identified a total of 987 differentially expressed genes (DEGs). GO enrichment analysis revealed that the DEGs were mainly associated with defense response to bacterium, innate immune response, and catalytic activity, suggesting that Lv-p62 may be transcriptionally linked to immune- and stress-related regulation. KEGG enrichment analysis identified significant enrichment of phagosome, ECM-receptor interaction, and cytoskeleton in muscle cells after FDR correction. These results suggest transcriptional alterations related to intracellular vesicle processing, extracellular matrix interactions, and cellular structural organization, indicating that Lv-p62 knockdown affects the expression of genes involved in immune-related clearance, autophagy-lysosome function, and metabolic pathways. The results of qRT-PCR of selected genes showed directional concordance with the transcriptomic data. Histopathological observation and TUNEL staining showed that Lv-p62 knockdown was associated with hepatopancreatic structural damage and increased TUNEL-positive signals. Collectively, these results suggest that Lv-p62 is associated with the transcriptional changes of immune- and redox-related genes, and that its knockdown is accompanied by histopathological structural alterations and increased TUNEL-positive signals in the hepatopancreas of L. vannamei.

title: Corneal Stiffening and Hyperosmolar Stress Associate With YAP1/TAZ Activation and Ocular Surface Inflammation in Dry Eye Disease.
abstract: To test whether corneal biomechanical remodeling and hyperosmolar stress activate Yes-associated protein 1 (YAP1)/transcriptional coactivator with PDZ-binding motif (TAZ) signaling in dry eye disease (DED), and whether YAP1/transcriptional enhanced associate domain (TEAD) activity is required for ocular surface inflammation in vivo. A desiccating stress (DS) mouse model was established using low humidity and scopolamine. Tear secretion, corneal fluorescein staining, and stromal stiffness were measured. YAP1/TAZ activity was assessed. DS mice received topical verteporfin (VP) or vehicle control. Human corneal epithelial cells (HCECs) were cultured on substrates of defined stiffness (8, 25, and 50 kPa) and exposed to hyperosmolar medium (500 mOsm) with YAP1 overexpression or knockdown. Public single-cell RNA sequencing data (GSE182582) were reanalyzed. DS reduced tear secretion and increased corneal fluorescein staining and central stromal stiffening. Decreased phosphorylated YAP1 (p-YAP1) and increased nuclear YAP1 indicated pathway activation. Topical VP reduced corneal injury and decreased YAP1, TAZ, connective tissue growth factor (CTGF), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6), while increasing p-YAP1. In HCECs, substrate stiffness and hyperosmolar stress increased YAP1 activation and inflammatory mediator expression; YAP1 silencing attenuated these responses, whereas YAP1 overexpression enhanced them. Single-cell reanalysis showed inflammatory enrichment in squamous epithelial cells with increased YAP1/WW domain-containing transcription regulator 1 (WWTR1) expression and Hippo pathway activation. Corneal stiffening and hyperosmolar stress are associated with YAP1/TAZ activation and epithelial inflammation in DED. YAP1/TEAD inhibition in DS mice ameliorates corneal injury and inflammatory signaling, supporting functional involvement. Pharmacologic modulation of YAP1/TEAD signaling may represent a therapeutic strategy for inflammation-dominant DED.

title: Molecular basis of anti-CD36 alloimmunization: transcriptomic evidence linking intronic splice-site mutations to CD36 loss-of-function.
abstract: CD36 deficiency is a genetic disorder that can lead to fetal/neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia or platelet transfusion refractoriness. While CD36 deficiency caused by exonic mutations are well established, the RNA splicing mechanism by intronic mutations remains poorly defined. CD36 deficiency patients were analyzed by long-read sequencing and haplotype analysis. RNA sequencing and allele-specific analysis validated mutation-splicing associations in patients. CD36 aberrant transcript plasmids were constructed and assessed by flow cytometry. Exome sequencing of healthy donors determined mutation frequencies. We found that population screening revealed a carrier frequency of approximately 2/800 for c.430-1G>C mutation and ~3/800 for c.429 + 3insG mutation among healthy Chinese donors. This study includes seven type I CD36 deficiency patients with PTR or FNAIT. Allele-specific analysis confirmed mutant allele enrichment in aberrant transcripts (P = 0.024). Long-read sequencing showed that one patient only had two intronic mutations (c.430-1G>C and c.429 + 3insG). Indicating intronic mutation was significantly linked to type I CD36 deficiency. Specifically, c.430-1G>C mutation induced aberrant exon 6 splicing, resulting in 17-bp pseudo-intron insertion or complete exon 6 skipping (28.6% or 30.3% skipped); the c.429 + 3insG mutation caused exon 5 skipping (38.3% skipped). Functional assays showed that the c.430-1G>C mutation led to complete loss of CD36 protein expression. This study establishes that intronic mutations alone can also induce CD36 deficiency by impairing mRNA splicing, thereby extending the known mutational landscape of CD36 deficiency and reinforcing the necessity of screening intronic mutations in diagnostic and pathogenetic investigations.

title: Community-based interventions to improve hepatitis C linkage to care among people with substance use disorders in Southwest Virginia: a pragmatic sequential cohort study.
abstract: In 2024, the reported hepatitis C virus (HCV) case rate in Roanoke City was nearly three times the rate of the state of Virginia, reflecting the disproportionate impact of the opioid epidemic in the region. Despite highly effective direct-acting antiviral therapies, substantial barriers to linkage to care (LTC) persist among individuals with substance use disorders (SUDs). While prior studies suggest that patient navigation and financial support may improve LTC, evidence from rural and underserved settings remains limited. This study aims to evaluate community-based interventions designed to improve HCV LTC among individuals with SUD in Southwest Virginia. We conducted a pragmatic, non-randomized, sequential cohort pilot study to evaluate the impact of iteratively refined community-based interventions on LTC. A total of 60 adults with detectable HCV RNA and SUD were enrolled sequentially into four cohorts (control and three intervention groups). All participants received peer support; intervention components were modified across cohorts to address observed barriers to care. The primary outcome was attendance at an outpatient HCV visit within 180 days of enrolment. LTC was 3/15 (20%) in both the control group and Intervention 1, increasing to 6/15 (40%) in Intervention 2 and 11/15 (73%) in Intervention 3. Exploratory analyses demonstrated significantly higher attendance in Intervention 3 than in the control group (73% vs. 20%, P = .009). Telehealth utilization and provision of prepaid phones were incorporated in the final cohort, which demonstrated the highest LTC rate. Multicomponent community-based interventions were associated with improved LTC among individuals with SUD. Although the non-randomized sequential design limits causal attribution, the progressive improvement across cohorts provides preliminary support for a potential benefit. Interventions incorporating community navigation, telehealth access, and communication support may help address barriers to HCV treatment engagement in underserved communities.

title: Diabetic retinal neurovascular unit injury: mechanisms, imaging evaluation, and integrated therapeutic strategies.
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) has long been regarded as an isolated retinal microvascular disease. Histopathological, molecular, imaging, and multi-omics evidence now supports disruption of retinal neurovascular unit (NVU) homeostasis as a central mechanism of DR, in which neuronal degeneration, reactive gliosis, and microvascular damage reinforce one another. This narrative review summarizes the anatomy and physiology of the NVU, its temporal evolution in DR, the molecular pathways of neurovascular crosstalk, quantitative imaging assessment, and integrated therapeutic strategies, and indicates where the evidence remains uncertain. PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science were searched from inception to July 2026 for reports on the retinal NVU in diabetes, and reference lists of retrieved articles were screened. Because this is a narrative rather than a systematic review, records were screened by the authors without a formal risk-of-bias assessment or quantitative synthesis. English-language reports addressing retinal NVU structure, diabetes-related injury mechanisms, imaging quantification, or NVU-directed interventions were eligible, and priority was given to human histopathological studies, prospective imaging cohorts, and translational intervention studies. Eighty-two references were included. Neurodegeneration is the earliest readily detectable change of NVU dysfunction in most cohorts, whereas microvascular injury amplifies retinal damage. Combined optical coherence tomography (OCT), OCT angiography (OCTA), and electroretinography (ERG) allow stage-specific quantification, and ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer (GCIPL) and deep capillary plexus vessel density (DVD) are among the most consistently reported early markers, although this evidence varies. Polyol pathway activation, AGE-RAGE and protein kinase C signaling, oxidative stress, HIF-1α/vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling, microglial STING and inflammasome activation, and non-coding RNA dysregulation jointly mediate bidirectional neurovascular injury. Vascular-targeted monotherapy cannot halt inner retinal neuronal loss, whereas multi-target strategies remain largely preclinical or at an early trial stage. In our interpretation, early neurodegeneration is the most readily detectable biomarker, microcirculatory damage acts as a disease amplifier, and complete NVU disintegration is the terminal common pathway. This framework is proposed to support ultra-early risk stratification and synergistic multi-target intervention, and is offered as one interpretation of a still-evolving evidence base rather than an established consensus.

title: Network toxicology, machine learning, single-cell analysis, and molecular docking reveal 6PPD/6PPD-Q-associated atrial fibrillation signatures.
abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most prevalent sustained arrhythmia worldwide, and environmental factors are increasingly recognized as contributors to its complex pathogenesis. The tire antioxidant N-(1,3-dimethylbutyl)-N'-phenyl-p-phenylenediamine (6PPD) and its oxidation product 6PPD-quinone (6PPD-Q) are emerging environmental contaminants with reported cardiotoxicity; however, their molecular relationship with AF remains unclear. This study aimed to identify potential molecular targets and pathways that link 6PPD/6PPD-Q exposure to AF using an integrated network toxicology and machine learning strategy. Multicohort atrial microarray datasets from patients with AF were integrated to identify AF-related genes using differential expression analysis, weighted gene coexpression network analysis, and GeneCards database screening. Putative targets of 6PPD/6PPD-Q were predicted using multiple in silico databases and intersected with AF-related genes. Network toxicology, enrichment analysis, machine learning with SHAP interpretation, single-cell RNA sequencing, and molecular docking were utilized to identify and characterize hub genes. Key targets were validated using qRT-PCR and western blotting in human cardiac fibroblasts. A mouse exposure model was further used to assess AF inducibility, duration, and cardiac gene expression in vivo. Sixteen putative AF-associated target genes of 6PPD/6PPD-Q were identified. Machine learning analysis highlighted four hub genes as key candidate hubs. Single-cell RNA analysis revealed cell type-specific expression, with enrichment in cardiomyocytes and vascular structural cells. Molecular docking predicted favorable binding interactions between 6PPD/6PPD-Q and the key target proteins. In vitro exposure to 6PPD or 6PPD-Q at the tested concentrations upregulated the mRNA and protein levels of all four candidate genes. In vivo exposure significantly increased pacing-induced AF inducibility, prolonged AF duration, and upregulated the expression of all these genes in cardiac tissues. These findings suggest that 6PPD and 6PPD-Q may contribute to AF by targeting specific genes and signaling pathways, with DDR1, BCHE, HTR2B, and KCNJ3 identified as core exposure-related hubs.

title: PHYHD1-mediated translational control regulates renal cell carcinoma progression.
abstract: The mechanisms underlying renal cell carcinoma (RCC) progression remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify phytanoyl-CoA dioxygenase domain containing 1 (PHYHD1) as a tumor suppressor that regulates translational homeostasis and RCC progression. Progressive PHYHD1 loss promotes tumor advancement and predicts poor prognosis, as revealed by integrative deep learning analysis of pan-cancer datasets. Restoring PHYHD1 suppresses tumor growth in RCC cell and patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models independently of its dioxygenase activity. Mechanistically, PHYHD1 interacts with translation elongation factor eEF1A1, alters its association with ribosomes, and restrains protein translation. Ribosome profiling and RNA-seq identify ceramide transporter 1 (CERT1) as a key effector of the PHYHD1-eEF1A1 axis. PHYHD1 depletion enhances CERT1 translation, whereas targeting CERT1 impairs proliferation of PHYHD1-deficient cells. These findings define a PHYHD1-eEF1A1-CERT1 axis that controls translation during RCC progression and highlight CERT1 as a potential therapeutic target in PHYHD1-deficient tumors.

title: Selective behavioral and prefrontal transcriptomic correlates of acute clozapine exposure in socially isolated mice.
abstract: Clozapine is an effective antipsychotic for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, but acute molecular responses to clozapine remain incompletely characterized. Social isolation rearing produces schizophrenia-relevant behavioral abnormalities and permits joint evaluation of housing and drug exposure. To characterize behavioral and prefrontal transcriptomic correlates of an acute clozapine challenge in socially isolated mice, reassess previously prioritized Ank3 and Nrxn1, and provide external cellular-context hypotheses for candidate genes. Male C57BL/6J mice were evaluated in a four-group housing-by-drug design using open-field, novel-object recognition and prepulse-inhibition tests. For a reproducible transcriptome-wide audit, 11 publicly retrievable prefrontal cortex libraries were re-quantified using a factorial DESeq2 model with false-discovery-rate control. Historical pairwise prioritization, network analysis, machine-learning screening, molecular docking and molecular-dynamics simulations were treated as exploratory analyses. Adult wild-type prefrontal cortex single-cell RNA-seq data were used for cellular localization, CellChat analysis and virtual knockout, whereas an embryonic cortical reference was used separately for CellOracle transcription-factor perturbation. Acute clozapine showed its clearest behavioral effect on isolation-associated hyperlocomotion, whereas recognition memory was not improved and prepulse-inhibition results varied by stimulus intensity. The primary DESeq2 analysis identified 56 housing-by-drug interaction genes at FDR <0.05; Lamb2 was the strongest FDR-supported transcriptomic signal. Nrxn1 showed directionally opposite changes in historical pairwise contrasts but did not reach FDR significance in the factorial model, whereas Ank3 showed no corresponding factorial support. In adult prefrontal cortex single-cell data, Lamb2 was concentrated in endothelial cells, while Ank3 and Nrxn1 were broadly detected in neuronal populations. Virtual Ank3 and Nrxn1 knockout profiles contained 16 and 15 significant non-target genes, respectively, with five shared genes and no significant reciprocal candidate effect. Embryonic CellOracle analyses identified model-dependent upstream transcription-factor sensitivity of Ank3 and Nrxn1. These findings define selective behavioral and prefrontal transcriptomic correlates of an acute clozapine challenge rather than generalized behavioral rescue or clinical treatment-response prediction. Lamb2 was the strongest FDR-supported signal in the primary model, whereas Ank3 and Nrxn1 remain exploratory computational candidates. The external single-cell and virtual-perturbation analyses provide testable cellular and regulatory hypotheses, not evidence of direct binding, causal regulation or clozapine-induced effects in vivo.

title: Polystyrene Nanoplastics Perturb Macrophage Mitochondrial Homeostasis and Inflammatory Responses: Evidence Implicating CPEB4.
abstract: Polystyrene nanoplastics (NPs) may affect macrophage function, but the relationships between inflammatory responses and mitochondrial alterations remain unclear. We combined exploratory analysis of public zebrafish intestinal single-cell RNA-sequencing data with transcriptomic, metabolomic, and experimental studies in RAW264.7 cells and primary mouse macrophages. In RAW264.7 cells, NPs increased reactive oxygen species (ROS), nitric oxide (NO), and the secretion of tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β), and interleukin-6 (IL-6). ROS and cytokine responses occurred at concentrations below those causing significant cytotoxicity in this cell line. A complex I-associated activity assay detected changes at lower NP concentrations than assays of cellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and the NAD+/NADH ratio. MitoSOX and JC-1 measurements further indicated changes in mitochondrial oxidant-sensitive fluorescence and membrane-potential-associated signals. Primary mouse macrophages showed concentration- and time-dependent responses, including increased TNF-α secretion. NPs exposure was also associated with reduced CPEB4 and INO80B protein abundance. CPEB4 knockdown increased ROS and reduced ATP at a later time point, whereas cellular thermal shift assay showed altered CPEB4 thermal behavior after NPs exposure. These findings identify inflammatory and mitochondrial responses associated with NPs exposure and implicate CPEB4 as a candidate contributor. However, they do not establish direct binding of intact NPs to CPEB4 or a causal role for CPEB4 or INO80B.

title: Artemisitene targets GLIS3 to inhibit the NF-κB-TNF signaling pathway and suppress bladder cancer cell growth.
abstract: Artemisia annua, a medicinal and edible herb best known for Artemisinin, exhibits broad pharmacological activities and considerable clinical value. However, its therapeutic potential in bladder cancer remains largely unexplored. Here, we systematically investigated the anti-bladder cancer efficacy of Artemisitene (ATT) in vitro and in vivo and delineated its underlying mechanisms. Using cell-based and animal models, we found that ATT robustly suppressed bladder cancer cell growth. Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic sequencing, combined with MST assays and transient transfection, revealed the mechanism of ATT inhibiting the progression of bladder cancer. In addition, we analysed single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets and performed virtual knockout experiments to investigate the expression pattern and potential functional role of the ATT target gene GLIS3 across different pathological stages of bladder cancer. GLIS3 expression was higher in tumour than in adjacent nontumor tissues in BLCA patients and was further elevated in intermediate/late stages (T3-T4) compared with early stages (T1-T2). Consistently, single-cell RNA-seq data showed that GLIS3 levels in epithelial cells were higher in T3-T4 than in T1-T2 BLCA. Moreover, in virtual GLIS3 knockout in BLCA epithelial cells negatively regulated TNF and NF-κB signalling pathways. ATT directly interacts with GLIS3 and destabilizes the protein, consequently suppressing the transcription of NF-κB and TNF. Mutation of GLIS3 at Arg-404 and Pro-411 markedly weakened its interaction with ATT and partly abrogated the pharmacological effects of ATT. Moreover, GLIS3 knockdown enhanced the inhibitory effect of Gem on bladder cancer cells, while ATT further potentiated Gem-mediated suppression of BLCA by downregulating GLIS3 expression. ATT binds to GLIS3 and decreases its protein stability, thereby suppressing the transcription of NF-κB and TNF, inducing apoptosis in bladder cancer cells, and inhibiting cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. These findings provide a mechanistic rationale for developing ATT as a potential therapeutic agent or dietary supplement for bladder cancer and expand the medicinal value of Artemisia annua derivatives.

title: TOMM5 is associated with oral cancer progression: a multi-omics analysis from single-cell atlas to in vitro validation.
abstract: Translocase of Outer Mitochondrial Membrane 5 (TOMM5), a mitochondrial outer membrane translocase subunit implicated in tumorigenesis, remains unexplored in oral cancer. Herein, we aimed to decipher the role of TOMM5 in oral cancer. This study comprehensively explored the expression profile, clinical significance, and functional roles of TOMM5 in oral carcinogenesis with global RNA-seq and microarray datasets. In vitro experiments were performed for evaluating the impact of TOMM5 knockdown on the biological functions of oral cancer cells. Distribution heterogeneity of TOMM5 expression and related cellular trajectory was analyzed through scRNA-seq. The therapeutic implications of TOMM5 for oral cancer were analyzed through drug sensitivity prediction and tumor immune dysfunction and exclusion (TIDE) scoring. TOMM5 was significantly overexpressed in oral cancer tissues and demonstrated moderate diagnostic accuracy. TOMM5 knockdown significantly suppressed aggressive biological behaviors of oral cancer cells. ScRNA-seq data revealed predominant TOMM5 expression in B cells, decreasing with differentiation, and linked distinct pathway activities to specific cellular compartments. High TOMM5 expression was linked to reduced immune cell infiltration and sensitivity to Paclitaxel/Vincristine. Overexpressed TOMM5 shows potential as a biomarker in oral cancer, correlating with tumor progression and immune infiltration.

title: FDX1 is associated with CALR abundance and JAK-STAT-related inflammatory signaling in myeloproliferative neoplasms.
abstract: Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) are driven by constitutive cytokine-receptor signaling, yet the metabolic programs associated with driver genotype and inflammatory remodeling remain incompletely defined. Here we integrated a 60-case clinical MPN cohort, the GSE174060 Affymetrix Human Transcriptome Array 2.0 microarray dataset, immune deconvolution, exploratory feature prioritization, the GSE228995 mouse single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) dataset, human-sample validation, and functional perturbation assays to investigate whether cuproptosis-related metabolism is associated with total calreticulin (CALR) abundance and Janus kinase-signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK-STAT)-related inflammatory signaling. GSE174060 included 36 samples: 6 essential thrombocythemia (ET), 11 polycythemia vera (PV), 9 primary myelofibrosis (PMF), 4 secondary myelofibrosis (SMF), and 6 healthy control (HC) samples. Clinically, CALR-mutated cases were enriched for thrombocytosis and distinctive megakaryocytic abnormalities, while inflammatory and fibrotic features tracked with higher interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). Microarray-based transcriptomic analyses identified an MPN-associated cuproptosis-related and immune-response program, and consensus clustering separated samples into exploratory transcriptomic clusters. Within this expression-derived partition, post hoc multi-algorithm feature prioritization recurrently retained FDX1 and CALR among genes associated with the Cluster 1-versus-Cluster 2 transcriptional contrast. Single-cell analyses localized Calr and Fdx1 across hematopoietic and immune populations and highlighted inferred JAK-STAT-associated communication potential. In human MPN samples, FDX1 and total CALR protein and mRNA levels were increased and accompanied by STAT5 phosphorylation and elevated inflammatory mediators. Functionally, FDX1 knockdown reduced total CALR abundance, STAT5 phosphorylation, cytokine release, sensitivity to copper-dependent cytotoxicity, and proliferation, whereas FDX1 overexpression showed the reciprocal pattern and was partly counteracted by ruxolitinib. These findings support an association between FDX1 perturbation, total CALR abundance, STAT5-associated signaling, and inflammatory output in MPN, but do not establish direct regulation of mutant CALR or mutant CALR-MPL signaling.

title: Immune-related molecular links between asthma and Alzheimer's disease identified by multi-omics, machine learning and single-cell analysis.
abstract: Epidemiological evidence suggests that asthma increases the risk of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet their shared immune-related molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to identify immune-associated molecular links between the two diseases. Gene expression datasets from GEO were analyzed to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and enriched pathways. WGCNA was used to detect immune-related modules, and machine learning algorithms were applied to refine candidate biomarkers. Mendelian randomization (MR) and experimental validation were conducted to investigate genetic associations and expression correlations. A logistic regression model and nomogram were constructed. Immune characteristics were further explored using GSEA, immune-cell signature analysis, and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq). CD163 and CHST6 were identified as cross-disease candidate genes. MR analyses showed nominal genetic associations of CD163 expression and plasma protein levels with asthma- and AD-related phenotypes, although these associations did not remain significant after FDR correction. CD163 and CHST6 also showed increased expression in independent asthma and AD mouse models. The combined diagnostic model showed good discrimination (AUC >0.87). Immune-cell signature analysis revealed tissue-dependent associations between the candidate genes and immune-related signatures. scRNA-seq revealed cell-type-specific expression patterns, with CD163 predominantly localized to myeloid-lineage populations, including microglia in AD and monocytes in severe asthma, whereas CHST6 showed context-dependent localization across glial and airway epithelial populations. CD163 and CHST6 represent potential cross-disease molecular candidates associated with asthma and AD. CD163 may reflect a systemic immune-associated signal, whereas CHST6 may reflect tissue- and context-dependent cellular changes. These findings provide a preliminary framework for further investigation of asthma-AD comorbidity and require validation in prospective and functional studies.

title: Integrative Bioinformatics Identifies TTN as a Potential Diagnostic Marker for Rheumatoid Arthritis.
abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease with heterogeneous clinical manifestations, and its molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. To identify core genes associated with RA and evaluate their diagnostic utility, with an emphasis on immune relevance and causality. Differential expression analysis and weighted gene coexpression network analysis were used to prioritize hub genes. Functional enrichment and protein-protein interaction analyses supported biological interpretation. A nomogram and receiver operating characteristic analysis were used to evaluate diagnostic performance, and immune cell infiltration was analyzed to identify immune-associated core genes. The causal effect of titin on the risk of RA was estimated using genome-wide association study data and two-sample Mendelian randomization. Validation was conducted in independent public transcriptomic datasets and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of synovial tissue. Titin (TTN) was prioritized as an RA-associated core gene and demonstrated favorable diagnostic performance. TTN expression was consistently higher in RA than in controls across validation datasets. Public external validation datasets supported increased TTN expression in RA, and scRNA-seq analysis suggested enrichment of TTN expression in synovial T cells. Mendelian randomization supported a causal association between genetically predicted TTN and RA risk. Collectively, evidence from bulk transcriptomics, immune cell infiltration profiling, single-cell localization, external validation, and genetic inference supports TTN as a previously underexplored candidate RA-associated biomarker with potential immune relevance. These findings extend current RA biomarker discovery by linking diagnostic performance with immune context and genetic support. Further mechanistic studies are needed to clarify whether TTN is involved in RA immunopathology or reflects inflammation-related tissue remodeling. Integrative analyses identify TTN as a potential RA-associated diagnostic biomarker requiring further experimental and clinical validation. Further studies are needed to clarify its mechanistic role and clinical utility in RA.

title: Single-Cell Transcriptomics Reveals Macrophage Dysfunction and cDC2 Activation in COPD: Candidate Biomarkers for Individualized Nursing Care.
abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality driven by dysregulated airway immunity. Macrophages and conventional type 2 dendritic cells (cDC2s) are central orchestrators of this process, yet their transcriptional heterogeneity at single-cell resolution and relationship to clinical severity remain incompletely characterized. We performed integrative analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from 45,708 lung immune cells combined with bulk microarray data from 236 lung tissue samples. After Harmony-based batch correction and graph-based clustering, 11 immune cell populations were annotated. Pseudobulk differential expression was performed using DESeq2, functional enrichment by gene set enrichment analysis against MSigDB Hallmark, KEGG, and GO:BP gene sets, and protein-protein interaction (PPI) network analysis using STRINGdb. Clinical correlation used Spearman rank correlation between hub gene expression and GOLD stage, FEV1% predicted, emphysema index, and DLCO%. Macrophages were depleted in COPD while cDC2s were 4.7-fold expanded. Macrophages exhibited 1,268 differentially expressed genes dominated by IFN-γ response (NES = 2.60) and TNFα/NF-κB activation (NES = 2.41), with concurrent loss of mitochondrial function (NES = -2.40) and lysosomal acidification (NES = -2.25). cDC2s showed strong TNFα/NF-κB (NES = 2.88) and JAK-STAT (NES = 2.36) activation. PPI analysis identified IFNG, IL1B, CCR7, GZMB, and NFKB1 as central hubs. Cross-dataset validation confirmed LRG1, CCR7, IRF4, and TIMP1 as clinically correlated biomarkers. This study identifies coordinated macrophage M1 polarization, metabolic dysfunction, and impaired efferocytosis in COPD, with cDC2-driven adaptive immune amplification. Eleven candidate biomarkers are proposed as targets for individualized nursing monitoring and precision respiratory care.
